+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 79.1
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Chapter Seven: The Antares Courtesy** The transfer vessel had no windows, which Arthur Neegan supposed was the point. He sat strapped into a padded couch that smelled faintly of ozone and someone else's tobacco, and he watched the only thing there was to watch: a small display screen bolted to the bulkhead, cycling through system diagnostics in patient green text. HULL INTEGRITY: NOMINAL CABIN PRESSURE: 1.02 ATM DRIVE CORE TEMP: 340 K AZRA CATALYST: STABLE That last line held his eye longer than the others. Somewhere aft of him, a few grams of the same grey-blue metal that lay beneath his forty hectares of red dust were quietly coaxing thorium into giving up its energy a million times faster than nature intended. A century ago, the trip from Mars orbit to wherever they were taking him would have been measured in months. Now the screen suggested it would be measured in hours. Progress, Arthur thought, and wondered whether progress had ever asked anyone's permission. The men who had come to his door had been very polite. That was what unsettled him most. They had worn charcoal uniforms with a starburst insignia in silver thread—Antares Diplomatic Corps, the patch said, though the sidearms on their hips had looked distinctly undiplomatic—and their captain had removed his cap before speaking. "Mr. Neegan. You are invited to a meeting." "And if I decline the invitation?" The captain had smiled, the way a man smiles at a child who asks why the sky is the color it is. "Then we would be obliged to explain, at some length, why declining would be unwise. I would prefer to spare us both." Arthur had gone. He was a mining engineer, not a hero, and he had noticed that the captain's men had already disconnected his communication relay. CABIN PRESSURE: 1.02 ATM DRIVE CORE TEMP: 341 K --- The room they brought him to was not what he expected. He had imagined something like the corporate offices in Bradbury Dome—chrome and glass and portraits of dead directors. Instead he found himself in a chamber paneled in actual wood, dark and oiled, with a carpet underfoot and a single low lamp. Beyond a broad viewport, Mars hung like a rusted coin against the black, and Arthur realized with a small lurch that he was looking at his home from a station he had not known existed. A woman sat behind a plain desk. She was perhaps sixty, with iron-colored hair cropped close and hands folded before her like someone waiting for a meal to be served. "Mr. Neegan. I am Director Veil. Please sit. Would you like coffee? Real coffee, I mean—Terran. Not the reconstituted business they serve you in the settlements." "I'd like to know why I'm here." "You are here because you are a very unlucky man who has been mistaken for a very lucky one." She poured two cups anyway. "Tell me what you know about Azra." Arthur sat. "It's a metal. Atomic number somewhere past anything on the old tables—they're still arguing. Put it near a radioactive material and the decay rate climbs. Put enough of it near the right material and you have a drive that reaches Jupiter in a week." "Or a weapon that reduces a city to glass in a heartbeat, using fuel that would otherwise sit harmlessly for ten thousand years. Yes." Veil slid a cup toward him. "Now tell me what you *don't* know." "That's a longer list." "Indeed. Here is one item on it. The known reserves of Azra, prior to your survey of last month, totaled approximately eleven metric tons, distributed across four claims controlled by three corporations and one government. Your vein, by the preliminary estimates that were—regrettably—transmitted over an unsecured channel, contains somewhere between forty and sixty tons." Arthur said nothing. The coffee was very good. "Do you understand what that means, Mr. Neegan? It means that every balance of power in this system was drawn up on the assumption of scarcity, and you have made Azra abundant. It means that the Terran Compact, the Belt Syndicates, the Martian Charter companies, and my own employers have all, in the last thirty days, begun to make plans that involve you. Most of those plans do not require you to remain alive." "And yours?" "Mine does. That is the offer." She leaned back. "The Antares Corps wishes to purchase your claim. Not lease it, not partner with you. Purchase it outright, for a sum I will write down rather than say aloud, because I dislike theatrics. In exchange, you and your daughter will be relocated to a world of your choosing under a name of your choosing, and you will never again have cause to think about Mars." Arthur looked at the figure she wrote. It was more money than the entire Bradbury settlement had generated in its history. "You said 'diplomatic corps.' I've never heard of a diplomat who travels with a platoon." "Diplomacy is the art of making violence unnecessary, Mr. Neegan. It is not the art of making it impossible." Veil's expression did not change. "The men who brought you here are the reason you were not brought somewhere else, by someone less inclined to offer coffee." "And if I refuse?" "Then you will be returned to your home tonight, unharmed, exactly as promised. And I estimate that within eleven days you will receive another visit, from a party that has not troubled to sew insignia on its uniforms." Beyond the viewport, Mars turned slowly. Somewhere on that small red disk, his daughter was asleep in a prefabricated house atop enough exotic metal to reorder human civilization. "You've thought about this more than I have," Arthur said. "I have thought about nothing else for a month. You have that advantage over me, Mr. Neegan—you have had a life." She stood. "You have until the station completes its next orbit. Ninety-four minutes. The coffee is yours." She left him alone with the cup, the view, and the slow, indifferent wheel of the planet below.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical competence and successfully captures the Asimovian style requested. The author effectively establishes the retrofuturistic atmosphere through details like the diagnostic readouts and the casual mention of thorium drives, while maintaining the clinical, measured tone characteristic of Asimov's work. The dialogue between Arthur and Director Veil is particularly well-crafted, feeling natural while efficiently conveying exposition and character. Veil's measured, almost bureaucratic menace ("Diplomacy is the art of making violence unnecessary... It is not the art of making it impossible") effectively establishes the stakes without melodrama. Arthur's responses feel authentic to his character as established - practical, cautious, but not naive. The world-building is economical yet vivid, successfully balancing Asimov's trademark "big picture" scope (the political implications of the Azra discovery) with intimate human stakes (Arthur's daughter, his modest life). The piece effectively hints at larger political machinations without overwhelming the immediate scene. However, the piece suffers from some predictability in its setup and resolution. The "mysterious powerful organization makes an offer you can't refuse" scenario, while well-executed, follows familiar beats. The characterization, while competent, lacks deeper psychological complexity - Arthur remains somewhat passive throughout, and Veil, despite her effective dialogue, doesn't transcend the "polite but dangerous bureaucrat" archetype. The prose is clean and professional but occasionally veers toward the mechanical. Some descriptions feel slightly overwrought ("Mars hung like a rusted coin") though this doesn't significantly detract from the overall effect. The pacing is well-controlled, building tension effectively toward the final decision point. The piece succeeds in its primary objectives: capturing Asimov's voice, advancing the plot meaningfully, and establishing the broader political stakes while maintaining focus on Arthur's personal dilemma. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 89.3
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Darkroom Revelations** The safelight turns everything the colour of the inside of a mouth. Red walls, red hands, red Elliot bent over the developer tray with his sleeves pushed up past the elbow, humming something I half-recognise—a Cocteau Twins song, maybe, the melody stretched thin and private. I've spent a whole semester watching him from across a classroom and I still can't say exactly what it is. The thrifted velvet blazer with the ripped lining. The silver rings on every finger, chipped black polish on the nails. The way he speaks so quietly that people lean toward him without realising they're doing it. I usually go for edges. Men who take up space, women who've decided exactly who they are and dare you to argue. Elliot is all softness and deliberation, and I have been telling myself for months that what I feel is aesthetic interest. Professional. He'd photograph beautifully. We've been in here three nights running. Professor Aldana paired us for the final—"alternative processes, push the medium"—and Elliot said *oh* in a way that could have meant anything, and I said *good, I don't have time to babysit* in a way I immediately regretted. He rocks the tray gently. The paper stays blank, then blooms. It's one of mine, a self-portrait, long exposure, my face smeared into three faces. "There you are," he says. "Or there you all are." "Which one do you think is me?" He considers it seriously. That's another thing. He never treats a question as rhetorical. "The one in the middle. The blurry one. The other two are just where you were and where you were going." I don't know what to do with that so I check my watch. Forty seconds. I want to reach past him and pull the print, because I always pull the print, because I'm the one who knows when things are done. Instead I fold my arms and let him do it. He lifts it with the tongs, lets it drip, slides it into the stop bath. His movements are careful in a way that makes me want to be careful too, which is not a thing I'm used to wanting. "Can I ask you something," he says, still looking at the tray, "and you can say no." "You can ask." "Do you think—" He stops. Hums a bar. Starts again. "When you look at me. What do you see?" It's not a flirt. I know what flirting sounds like; I've done enough of it. This is something more like a hand held out in the dark to check if the wall is still there. "Honestly?" "That's the only reason I'd ask." "I see someone who dresses like the boys I liked at seventeen and moves like nobody I've ever met." Too much. I keep going anyway. "I see someone who's very good at this and doesn't know it yet." He laughs, barely. "That's not what I meant. But thank you." "What did you mean?" The print goes into the fixer. He sets the tongs down. When he speaks his voice is even quieter, so I have to step closer, so close I can smell the vinegar sharpness of the stop bath on his hands. "I don't think I'm a boy. I'm not sure I'm—anything else either. I've just been noticing lately that when people say *he*, there's this half-second where I have to remember it's me they're talking to." He pushes his hair back. "I haven't said that out loud before. To anyone. I think the light in here makes it easier. Nothing looks real." Every instinct I have says *take charge*. Say the right thing, confidently, fix it, lead. I open my mouth and what comes out is: "Okay." "Okay?" "Okay. Thank you for telling me." I hear myself sounding like a pamphlet and hate it. "I mean—what do you want me to do with that? Do you want me to use something else? Do you want me to just know?" "I don't know yet." He looks at me for the first time since he started. His eyes are enormous in the red. "I think I wanted to hear how it sounded." "How does it sound?" "Terrifying." A breath. "Right." I should step back. I'm twenty-five and he's nineteen and he's just handed me something that isn't mine to hold. But I'm also aware, with a clarity that scares me a little, that I am *not* stepping back, and that the reason has nothing to do with wanting to help. I thought I knew the shape of my own desire. I thought it needed a defined outline to attach to. And here is Elliot, deliberately blurring, and I want him more, not less, and I don't have a word for what that makes me. "I don't usually—" I start. "Like people like me?" "I don't usually not know what I'm doing." He smiles. It's the first fully unguarded thing I've seen from him. "I don't either. I mean I never know what I'm doing. But I usually know I don't know." We're both looking at the print in the fixer. Three of my faces, settling into permanence. Behind us the timer ticks for nothing. "Can I," I say, and I stop, because I realise I'm about to ask and not tell. Because I want him to be the one who says yes. "Can I hold your hand. Just that." He doesn't answer. He just turns his palm up, wet and cold and smelling of chemicals, and I put mine over it. His rings press into my fingers. His thumb moves once, slowly, across my knuckle, and I feel it in my throat. "You're humming again," I say. "Am I?" "You do it when you're waiting for something to come up." "Oh." He doesn't stop. "I guess I'm waiting." The print is ready. Neither of us moves to pull it. In the red light we stand there, not developed yet, not fixed, and for once in my life I let the moment tell me when it's done.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates sophisticated literary craft in exploring complex themes of gender identity, attraction, and vulnerability. The darkroom setting functions brilliantly as both literal space and metaphor for development and revelation. The author skillfully uses the photography process as a structural and thematic framework, with particularly effective moments like "not developed yet, not fixed" serving as both technical description and emotional metaphor. The characterization is nuanced and authentic. Dani's voice feels genuinely conflicted - her usual assertiveness challenged by unfamiliar territory, creating believable internal tension. The portrayal of Elliot's gender questioning is handled with sensitivity and realism, avoiding both oversimplification and melodrama. The age gap and power dynamics are acknowledged without being heavy-handed. The prose quality is consistently high, with evocative imagery like "the colour of the inside of a mouth" and "moves like nobody I've ever met." The writing maintains an intimate, contemplative tone that suits the confessional atmosphere. Dialogue feels natural and serves character development effectively, particularly Elliot's tentative revelation and Dani's struggle to respond appropriately. The emotional complexity is well-executed, exploring Dani's confusion about her own identity and attraction patterns without providing easy answers. The piece avoids rushing toward resolution, instead sitting with uncertainty in a way that feels mature and realistic. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the metaphorical language borders on being slightly overwrought, and the ending, while poetic, risks being somewhat precious. However, these are minor concerns in an otherwise accomplished piece that successfully balances literary ambition with emotional authenticity. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 86.8
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Stolen Moments in Roma** **I. Trevi, 9:14 a.m.** The Vespa came around the corner of Via delle Muratte like a wasp with a grudge. Ben Whitcombe, senior lecturer in Renaissance history, University of Exeter, saw none of it. He was reading about Nicola Salvi's travertine and stepping backward into the road with the serene confidence of a man who trusted pavements. Brakes shrieked. Something hot brushed his elbow. A helmet tipped back to reveal a woman with a jaw like a dare and eyes the colour of espresso left too long on the stove. "*Ma sei scemo? Ti sembra il posto per leggere?*" "I—*mi dispiace*—terribly—*sono*—" He consulted the phrasebook in his head and found it empty. "*Sono un cretino*." She stared. Then she laughed, one sharp bark that startled a pigeon. "At least you know yourself. Most men take forty years." She killed the engine. "Alessandra. You almost died. Congratulations." "Ben. Thank you? I think." She looked at the guidebook in his hands, the linen jacket, the sensible shoes, and something behind her eyes made a decision. "Get on." "I'm sorry?" "You want to see Roma. That book shows you where the Germans stand. I show you the city." She patted the seat. "Or you can go back to almost dying alone." He got on. **II. Campo de' Fiori, 10:02** She wove through the market like she owned the lease on it. At a fruit stall she argued with a man twice her width about the price of apricots, lost the argument, and walked away with one anyway, tucked into her jacket while the man's back was turned. "Did you just—" "He overcharges tourists. I balance the universe." She bit the apricot and handed him the other half. "You're an accomplice now, *professore*." The fruit was warm from the sun and appallingly sweet. He ate it. **III. Somewhere off Via Giulia, 11:30** She led him through a green door that was very clearly not for the public, up four flights of a palazzo staircase, and out onto a roof where laundry snapped like flags. Rome spread below them, ochre and gold, the dome of St Peter's floating over it all like a held breath. "Who lives here?" "No idea." She lay down on the warm tiles. "Sit. You're blocking my view of the Pope's house." He sat. His heart was doing something unscholarly. He noticed a wooden clothes peg had migrated from the washing line into her back pocket. She noticed him noticing. "Everything in this city was stolen from somewhere," she said. "The obelisks, the marble, the gods. Rome is a thief that got old and respectable." She squinted at him. "You would look better without the jacket." He took off the jacket. **IV. Testaccio, 1:15 p.m.** Lunch was a bar with no sign and a proprietor who kissed Alessandra on both cheeks and then held her at arm's length like a suspicious parcel. "Marco," she said. "This is Ben. He's English. Be gentle." Marco poured two glasses of something amber and leaned across the zinc toward Ben while she went to the toilet. "Listen, *inglese*. I've known her since she was fifteen and stealing my ashtrays. She is—" he searched for the word and settled for a gesture, hands opening like a magician's. "She takes what she likes. Sometimes she gives it back. Sometimes you don't know it's gone until you're home." He tapped Ben's chest, twice, over the heart. "Guard this. And your pockets." "Marco is jealous," Alessandra said, returning, "because I stole his girlfriend in 2009." "You didn't *want* her. You just wanted to see if you could." "Exactly." She drank Ben's glass instead of her own. "*Andiamo*." Ben checked his wallet on the way out. Still there. He was almost disappointed. **V. Via Appia Antica, 3:40** She rode the ancient road faster than any Roman legionary would have sanctioned. Ben's arms were around her waist because physics required it, and because physics, he was discovering, was an excellent excuse. Cypress trees blurred. Tombs of the forgotten flickered past. "Faster?" she shouted. "God, no." She went faster. He found he was laughing. Actually laughing, mouth open, wind tearing at it, a sound he hadn't produced since before the divorce, before the sabbatical committee, before he'd become a man who read about fountains instead of standing in them. **VI. Aventine, 6:20** The keyhole in the door of the Knights of Malta, the one that frames St Peter's like a jewel. There was a queue. Alessandra walked past it, said something to the guard that made him blush, and pulled Ben to the front. "What did you tell him?" "That you were dying. Nobody argues with a dying Englishman. It's the accent." He put his eye to the keyhole. Green hedges, and at the end of them, perfectly centred, the dome. It looked like a secret he had been let in on. When he stepped back she was very close. She smelled of petrol and apricots. "Well?" she said. "I don't understand you at all." "Good. Understanding is for guidebooks." **VII. Trevi, 9:50 p.m.** The fountain roared, lit gold, tourists throwing their coins over their shoulders. They stood where the day had begun. "Tomorrow I'm back on the bike at seven," she said. "Packages. Real life." "Right. Of course." He put his hands in his pockets and stopped. Felt again. "My watch." "Which watch?" "My father's. It was on my—" He looked at his bare wrist and then at her, and something cold slid through him. Marco's hands, opening. She held it up between two fingers, the strap dangling, the face catching the fountain light. He had never felt it leave him. "When?" "The roof. You were looking at the Pope." She didn't hand it over. "Marco was right about me, you know. I take things. I don't always know why. It's a kind of—" she shrugged "—hunger." "And do you give them back?" "Sometimes." She stepped in, fastened the watch around his wrist herself, her fingers slow on the buckle. "Only if I want to see the owner again." She kissed him then, brief and unfair, and was on the Vespa before he'd finished being kissed. "Seven o'clock," she called over the engine. "Here. Bring the book. I want to see what else they got wrong." She was gone into the noise of Rome. Ben stood by the fountain a long time, one hand on his father's watch, the other in his jacket pocket, where he discovered—quite without knowing how it had got there—a single wooden clothes peg.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and creative execution within the contemporary romance genre. The author successfully creates two distinct, compelling characters whose personalities emerge naturally through action and dialogue rather than exposition. Alessandra's kleptomaniacal tendencies are woven seamlessly into the narrative, manifesting in escalating acts from the stolen apricot to the climactic watch theft, while Ben's transformation from buttoned-up academic to willing accomplice feels organic and well-paced. The structure works effectively, using numbered vignettes that create a cinematic quality while maintaining narrative momentum. The time stamps add authenticity and help track the characters' emotional journey throughout the day. The writing demonstrates sophisticated control of voice and tone, balancing humor with genuine romantic tension. The dialogue is particularly strong, capturing distinct speech patterns for each character. Alessandra's mix of Italian and English feels natural rather than forced, while Ben's awkward politeness evolves convincingly. The secondary characters like Marco serve their purpose well, providing both exposition and external perspective on the protagonists. The imagery is vivid without being overwrought - descriptions like "eyes the colour of espresso left too long on the stove" and "Rome spread below them, ochre and gold" create atmosphere without slowing pace. The author demonstrates restraint in avoiding purple prose while maintaining literary quality. The kleptomania subplot is handled with particular skill, building from minor infractions to the emotionally significant watch theft. The revelation and return of the watch provides genuine emotional payoff and character development for both protagonists. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose edges toward being overly polished for the raw energy the story is trying to capture, and Ben's transformation, while believable, happens quite rapidly within the single day timeframe. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Last Outpost ## Chapter Four: Neat The Outpost hums the way it always does on a third-shift evening: recyclers ticking behind the walls, Dorran arguing with the dart board, the Kessel twins pretending they aren't holding hands under table six. The lights are low and amber because I set them low and amber. People drink more honestly in amber. I'm wiping the bar when the door cycles and the stranger comes in. Tentacled dreads, the long kind, the sort that usually drape neat down someone's back. Hers stick out at angles, twitching like they haven't agreed on a direction. Her jacket is good quality and badly torn. She takes the stool at the far end, the one nobody takes because it wobbles, and sets both hands flat on the counter. "Vega whisky, neat." Her voice is scraped thin. "Better make that a double." I pour it. Real Vega, not the belt-brewed stuff we pass off on the miners who won't know. Something about her says she'd know. "Rough transit?" I ask. She drinks half of it before answering. "Rough everything." "That's a real ship you flew in on. I felt the docking clamps." I pick the rag back up, find the spot I was working on. There's a ring there, an old one, worn into the varnish by a thousand glasses. It never comes out. I wipe it anyway. "Most people who fly real ships don't stop here. We're not on the way to anywhere." "That's the appeal." "Fair." One of her dreads curls toward the door, then back. She notices me noticing. "Sorry. They do that. Autonomic." She finishes the glass and pushes it half an inch toward me. "Same again." "You want a bowl of stew with that? Vek made it. It's mostly potato but he's proud of it." "Just the whisky." I pour. Wipe. Down at the dart board, Dorran lands a triple and cheers loud enough to rattle the bottles. The stranger flinches like the sound has weight. "Nettle," I say. "Nets, if you're staying long enough to be a friend." "Osk." A pause. "That'll do for now." "That'll do fine. Most of my regulars aren't using the names their mothers gave them either." She almost smiles. It doesn't take. "Is there a comms relay here? Long range?" "There's a relay. Long range is generous. It talks to the mining beacon and the mining beacon talks to the supply run every eleven days." "Eleven days." "Give or take." Her hands come off the counter and grip the edge of it instead. "That's not going to work." "It usually doesn't, for people in a hurry. That's how I know you're in a hurry." I lean into the rag. Same spot. The ring stays. "You want to tell me what you're running from, or you want me to guess? I'm good at guessing. It's one of the talents that offsets the flaws." "What flaws?" "I'm nosy. I'm stubborn. I ask questions of people who order doubles." She looks at me for a long moment. Her eyes are dark all the way through, no whites, and there's a ring of pale gold at the center that contracts when she's thinking. It contracts now. "I was a courier," she says. "Independent. Sealed cargo, no questions, half up front. Standard." "Standard." "Three jumps ago I got boarded. Not pirates. Organized. Uniforms with the patches stripped off. They took the cargo." She turns the empty glass in a slow circle. "Except they didn't take all of it. One crate was in the cabin, not the hold. They missed it. And now the people who paid me think I sold them out, and the people who boarded me know they're one crate short." "So everybody wants you." "Everybody wants the crate. I'm just the thing standing next to it." I wipe the ring. It occurs to me that I've been wiping it for a while. I don't stop. "What's in the crate?" "I don't know. Sealed cargo. No questions." She says it like a prayer she's stopped believing in. "It's heavier than it should be." "Where is it now?" "On my ship. Docked at your clamp four." "Osk." I set my voice down carefully. "Who paid you?" She hesitates. Then: "A firm called Halvard Meridian. Out of the Cassine reach." The rag stops. Just for a second. Then it moves again, small circles, same spot, and I hope she's too tired to have caught it. Halvard Meridian. I haven't heard those two words together in six years. I left a whole life behind so I wouldn't have to. "Never heard of them," I say. "You're a bad liar." "I'm actually a very good liar. I just wasn't trying." I fold the rag, unfold it. "How far behind you are they?" "The boarders? I don't know. Halvard?" Her dreads sag, all of them at once, like a held breath let go. "Two days. Maybe less. I burned everything I had getting out here and they've got better engines." Two days. I look down the bar. Dorran's lining up another throw. The Kessel twins have given up pretending and are just holding hands on top of the table now. Vek is in the back singing to his stew. Old Mira's asleep in the corner booth with her boots on the seat because she knows I won't wake her. This place tolerates me. That's the word I use, when I'm being honest with myself. Tolerates. I've never given it a reason to do anything else. "You can't stay here," I say. "I know." "You can't leave, either. Not on a ship they can outrun." "I know that too." She looks at the glass. "Third one?" I don't pour it. I put the rag down, finally, and the ring is still there, and it's always going to be there. "Finish your drink," I tell her. "Then show me the crate."

The world-building feels organic rather than forced. The dialogue carries the story effectively, meeting the 60% target while feeling natural and purposeful. Nets' voice is consistent throughout - world-weary but caring, with a bartender's practiced ability to read people. Her observations about the stranger's expensive whiskey preferences and the way she notices autonomic dread movements show character through action rather than exposition. The conflict setup is well-executed. Osk's predicament - caught between the people who hired her and those who robbed her - creates genuine tension. The revelation of Halvard Meridian and Nets' subtle reaction (the stopped rag, claiming to be a good liar who "just wasn't trying") hints at deeper connections without over-explaining. This restraint serves the narrative well. Character development feels earned. The writing avoids melodrama while building genuine stakes. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Gone South — Chapter Two: Tuesday, Apparently** The strap slips off my shoulder for the hundredth time and I hitch it back up without thinking, which is how I know I've been walking a while. My body's on autopilot. My brain's still somewhere around Hattiesburg, replaying the sound of a car door shutting behind me and a man saying *good luck, kid* in a voice that meant *you're not my problem anymore*. New Orleans smells like wet garbage and beignets. I hadn't expected that. I hadn't expected anything, honestly, because I did not plan this. I *executed* this. There's a difference, and the difference is that right now I have forty-one dollars, a phone at nine percent, and a backpack I packed in the dark with what turned out to be three T-shirts, no socks, and Mom's good phone charger. Sorry, Mom. Actually, no. Not sorry. *She said it's a phase.* Two days later I still can't get past that word. Phase. Like I'm the moon. I find a bench in a square with a cathedral at one end and a guy painted entirely silver at the other. Tourists drift by in a herd. I sit and try to look like someone who is supposed to be here, which is a skill I've been practicing my whole life. "You're doing the thing." I look up. A girl — maybe seventeen, maybe twenty, hard to tell under the hoodie — is standing over me eating a hot dog she definitely didn't pay for, based on how fast she's eating it. "What thing." "Looking around like the ground's going to open up. It won't. It's just New Orleans." She sits down without asking. "You got here today." "How do you—" "Backpack's too full. Nobody who's been here more than a week carries that much. It gets stolen or it gets heavy." She wipes her hand on her jeans. "I'm Dee." "Taylor." She didn't ask if that was my real name, which I appreciated more than I could say. Back home, everyone knew exactly what my name was and exactly what shape they'd decided I was, and there was no room to breathe inside all that knowing. Here, nobody knew anything. That was the terrifying part. That was also the point. "Where you from, Taylor?" "Tennessee." "Yikes." "Yeah." She laughs, and it's a good laugh, a real one, and I feel something in my chest unclench about half an inch. --- Dee shows me where the public bathroom is that doesn't require a purchase. She shows me which tourists tip street kids and which ones call the cops. She talks fast and never quite finishes a story — every time I ask a follow-up she's already three subjects down the road. "So how long have you been here?" I ask, hitching the strap. It slides right back down. I'm starting to take it personally. "Long enough." Then, before I can push: "You should ditch half that stuff. Seriously. Speed's more useful than socks." "I don't have socks." She stares at me. "Okay, you're a disaster. Come on." *Don't trust her*, says the part of my brain that sounds like the school counsellor. *This is exactly the kind of thing. Concerning behavioural pattern. Following strangers.* *Yeah, well*, says the rest of me, *I'm two states from anyone who's ever hurt me, and she's the first person in forty-eight hours who hasn't looked at me like I broke something.* I follow her. --- We end up on the river. The Mississippi is fat and brown and moving faster than it looks, and there's a bunch of kids on the steps who all know Dee and all look at me the way a dog sniffs a new dog. One of them, a tall boy with a tattoo of a spoon on his neck, gives Dee a nod that's got a whole conversation folded into it. "Who's the fresh one?" "Taylor. From Tennessee." "Yikes." "That's what I said." I sit on the concrete and the strap gives up entirely and the bag slumps against my hip. I let it. "So what's your deal?" Spoon Boy asks. "Parents?" Here it is. The moment I've been dreading and wanting in equal parts since the highway. In Tennessee, saying it out loud had detonated my entire life. I open my mouth and wait to see what comes out. "I told them I'm not a girl." My voice is steadier than I expected. "They said I could be whatever I wanted as long as I did it in my room with the door shut and never mentioned it at dinner." Nobody gasps. Nobody prays. Spoon Boy just says "Cool," in the tone of someone confirming a lunch order, and passes me half a granola bar. I hold it and try very hard not to cry over a granola bar. Dee's watching me. There's something in her face that wasn't there before — like a window left open a crack. "Mine wasn't like that," she says, quiet, not to the group. "Mine was worse." "What happened?" The window shuts. "Long story. You hungry? I know a place that throws out sandwiches at four." --- Later, when the light's going orange and the river's turned the color of an old penny, Dee's phone buzzes and she flinches like it bit her. She looks at the screen, goes pale, puts it face down on the step. Then she picks it up and puts it in her pocket. Then she takes it out and turns it off entirely. "Everything okay?" "Yeah." She's not looking at me. "Somebody who shouldn't have this number." I think about my own phone, dying in my bag, full of missed calls I haven't listened to. I think about how Dee said *long enough* like it was a number she'd rather not say out loud. I think about how you can be sitting right next to someone and still have no idea what they're running from. *You don't know her. She could be anyone. She could be worse than what you left.* *Or she could be exactly what you are. Just further down the road.* "Hey," she says finally. "You got anywhere to sleep?" "No." "Okay." She stands, and she's back — fast, bright, unfinished. "I know a place. It's not great. Bring your stupid heavy bag." I stand too. I hitch the strap up onto my shoulder. It stays there for almost a full block.

+ Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 85.5
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**My Apocalypse Buddy** Midas woke, as he did every morning, to the sound of a koala having an opinion. "CAN'T BEAT THE REAL THING," said Chewy, from the shelf. "Nobody asked you," said Midas. Chewy was an animatronic koala of the sort once given to children by relatives who did not have to live with it. He had glass eyes, a mouth on a small hinge, and, somewhere in his stuffing, a chip that remembered forty-one advertising slogans from a world that had stopped existing around the time the lights went out and stayed out.\* He was Midas's oldest friend, which said less about Chewy than it did about Midas. *\*Nobody was certain what had ended civilisation. The general consensus was that it had been going to happen anyway and someone had pressed the button early to save time.* They lived in a car wash. It had a roof, which placed it in the top percentile of available housing, and a row of enormous blue brushes that Midas had spent one whole winter convinced were watching him. "Right," said Midas, sitting up. "Situation." He liked to begin the day this way. It gave the impression of a plan. The situation was as follows. They had four tins of something labelled only PRODUCT, half a bag of rice that had started, alarmingly, to move, and Chewy's batteries were dying. Midas knew this because the koala had begun delivering his slogans slowly, in the voice of a man dictating a will. "We need batteries," said Midas. "BATTERIES... NOT... INCLUDED," said Chewy. "I *know* they're not included. That's the problem." Across the river stood the Retail Park, which in the Before Times had sold everything and now sold nothing to anyone with a crowbar. Midas had avoided it for two years on the grounds that it was full of Retailers, which is what people called the folk who had moved in and developed, over time, strong views about outsiders and a great many sharpened trolley poles. "In and out," said Midas. "Hardware aisle. Batteries. Nobody sees us." He put Chewy in his rucksack so only the head poked out, and set off. --- The first thing to go wrong was the bridge, which had, since Midas last looked, gone. Not collapsed. Simply *gone*, in the way useful things do, and in its place hung a rope with a sign reading TOLL and, beneath the sign, a man who owned the rope. "Toll's a tin," said the man. Midas paid a tin of PRODUCT and crossed hand over hand, a koala murmuring "EVERY LITTLE HELPS" into his left ear. Halfway across, the man shouted that the toll was two tins on Tuesdays. Midas did not know what day it was. Nobody did. It had been one of the first things to go.\*\* *\*\*With the calendar went Tuesday, and with Tuesday, in a sense, went hope. Very little is possible without Tuesdays.* The second thing to go wrong was that the Retail Park was having a service. Midas crept through what had once been Homeware and found, in the great atrium where the escalators had frozen halfway like a metaphor, sixty Retailers kneeling before a vending machine. It glowed from within by some cruel miracle of surviving solar panel, and it hummed. The Retailers hummed back. Midas would have retreated. He had most of a retreat done. But Chewy—sensing perhaps a kindred spirit, or perhaps just the last of his voltage—chose that moment to announce to the congregation: "ASK YOUR DOCTOR IF IT'S RIGHT FOR YOU." Sixty heads turned. There is a particular silence that occurs when many people who believe in a machine hear a *different* machine talk. It is a hopeful silence. It is also brief. "It speaks," said a woman at the front, wearing a lanyard of many colours and, Midas gathered, the authority that went with it. "It's a toy," said Midas. "IT'S NOT JUST A TOY," said Chewy, which was untrue, and which nobody present, Chewy included, fully understood. But it *sounded* like prophecy, and prophecy, like bridges, tends to be owned by whoever's holding the rope. What followed was a Theological Dispute, which in the Aftermath meant trolley poles. The Retailers split roughly into those who felt the koala was a herald of the Machine, those who felt it was a rival god and should be burned, and a small pragmatic faction who just wanted to know if it had any batteries in it. Midas resolved the matter by running. He ran through Homeware, through Garden, through a section that had once sold televisions and now sold a view of the sky. He ran past the hardware aisle, noting in the part of his brain not occupied with screaming that this was where the batteries would have been. He ran up a stopped escalator and along a gantry and, when the gantry ended, kept running briefly out of momentum, and then fell into the river. --- The river brought him home. It was, he reflected, drifting past the tollman's second invoice, the only thing that ever had. The current knew where the car wash was. It delivered him to the drainage grate beneath the great blue brushes, and he crawled out and lay on the concrete for some time. Chewy was not with him. Chewy had left the rucksack during the Dispute in the traditional manner of things pulled out of rucksacks by mobs. Midas grieved. He did this by eating a tin of PRODUCT and staring at the empty shelf. He was still staring when, at dusk, a goat walked into the car wash. It was one of the feral goats from Garden, and tied around its neck with a rainbow lanyard was a koala. The koala had lost an ear and most of his stuffing, one glass eye hung by a thread, and round his remaining ear was a charcoal note: THIS IS YOURS. WE VOTED. DO NOT COME BACK. It occurred to Midas that the Retailers had solved a problem nobody in the Aftermath had solved—the problem of delivery—and that they had done it with faith and livestock, and that this was probably how the vending machine had got started. He set Chewy on the shelf. Lopsided. Leaking. One-eyed. Home. "Well," said Midas. "That was a day." The little hinge moved. From the last of his charge, slowly, like a man dictating a will, Chewy said: "TERMS... AND... CONDITIONS... APPLY." And then, for the first time in Midas's memory, nothing at all. Midas sat with him while the goat ate the rice. In the morning—in case you were wondering—the mission was batteries.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, successfully capturing his dry wit, footnoted observations, and philosophical undercurrents. The author effectively creates a post-apocalyptic world that feels both bleak and absurdly humorous, maintaining the required tone throughout. The story structure follows the prompt precisely: deliberation about the mission (getting batteries), the inevitable complications (missing bridge, religious dispute, chase scene), and return home worse for wear. The characterization is particularly strong - Midas emerges as a believably hapless protagonist whose bad luck feels authentic rather than contrived, while Chewy functions brilliantly as both comic relief and emotional anchor through his deteriorating advertising slogans. The prose demonstrates genuine elegance, with memorable phrases like "Nobody was certain what had ended civilisation. The general consensus was that it had been going to happen anyway and someone had pressed the button early to save time." The footnotes are well-executed Pratchett pastiche without feeling derivative. The world-building is economical but vivid - the car wash home, the Retail Park theology, the missing Tuesdays all create a coherent post-apocalyptic landscape. The dialogue, while limited, serves its purpose effectively. Chewy's deteriorating slogans provide both humor and pathos, while Midas's interactions feel natural. The story avoids purple prose and overwrought emotion, maintaining the dry tone even in moments of loss. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - neither falsely optimistic nor gratuitously dark. Chewy's final "TERMS... AND... CONDITIONS... APPLY" before dying is both funny and genuinely touching. The circular structure (ending with another battery mission) provides satisfying closure while suggesting the ongoing nature of survival. Minor weaknesses include some predictable beats in the middle section and perhaps slightly rushed pacing during the Retail Park sequence, but these don't significantly detract from the overall achievement. The piece succeeds as both Pratchett homage and original post-apocalyptic fiction. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**The Sewin Hour** The bell above the door of Pugh & Daughter went off like a gunshot, and a man in sunglasses and a coat too expensive for Llandeilo flattened himself against the Welsh History shelf. "Don't mind me," he said. "I'm browsing." Nerys didn't look up from the receipts. "You're breathing on the Gerald of Wales." "He's had worse." He tilted his head toward the window, where two men with long lenses were jogging past the butcher's. "Could you possibly—the blind?" "It's stuck." "Right." He took off the sunglasses, and there it was: the face from the side of every bus in Cardiff. Julian Ashcombe. Three franchises, one divorce, a smile that had been called *devastating* by a magazine she'd definitely not bought. He aimed it at her now. Full beam. "You know who I am," he said. "I know you're leaning on a first edition." He straightened, which put him in the middle of the shop with nothing to hide behind, and she watched him decide to make that look intentional. He picked up a book at random. *Sheep Diseases of the Cambrian Uplands.* "Fascinating," he said. "It is, actually." "I'm sure." He turned a page. "You're not going to ask for a photo." "Did you want me to?" "No. God, no. It's just—people usually do." He laughed, and it was a good laugh, a practised one, and she felt it land somewhere under her ribs like a dropped coin. She frowned at the receipts harder. "It's nice. Refreshing. To be treated like a normal person." "You're not a normal person. You're a fire hazard blocking my exit." "That's fair." Outside, a lens flashed against the glass. He flinched—a small thing, a genuine thing—and she felt her own hand move before she'd approved it, sliding the ladder along the rail so that it sat across the window like a shutter. "There," she said. "Your blind." "Thank you." He said it quietly, without the beam. Then the beam came back, twice as bright, as if to make up for the lapse. "You know, most people would've charged me for that." "I'm considering it." "What's your name?" "Nerys." "Nerys." He said it like he was tasting it. "Beautiful. Is it—" "If you're about to tell me it's beautiful, I'll take the ladder away." His mouth actually opened and nothing came out. She'd never seen that happen to a man on a bus advert. He shut it again and put down the sheep book and picked up another, and this time he actually looked at it, and something in his shoulders changed. "Hang on," he said. "This is *Falkus.* You've got a first *Sea Trout Fishing*." "Bottom shelf, left. You're a fisherman?" "I was. Am. My grandfather used to bring me up here, actually—well, Llangadog way. Night fishing the Tywi for sewin. I've not done it in—" He stopped. Did the maths. Looked briefly appalled. "Fourteen years." "That's a long time between casts." "Tell me about it." He turned the book over in his hands like he'd forgotten there were photographers outside at all. "Do you fish?" "Every night the river's right, from June through. I've a beat below the bridge." "You *don't.*" "I do." "What are you throwing? No, let me guess." He squinted at her. "Something small and black and stubborn." She felt her face do something she didn't sanction. "Size ten. Stoat's tail." "I *knew* it." He was grinning now, and it wasn't the bus-advert one; it was lopsided and it showed a slightly crooked tooth that the magazines must airbrush, and she thought, oh, that's the real one, and then she thought, stop it, Nerys. "I used to tie my own," he said. "Badly. Grandad said my hackles looked like they'd been in a fight." "Mine still do." "Liar." "No, honestly. I've a box in the back that would make you weep." "Show me." She didn't move. He took a step closer, then seemed to hear himself and took it back. "Sorry. That was—I don't know why I said that. I don't generally just demand people show me their fly boxes." "I should hope not." "It's just—" He ran a hand through hair that probably had a person assigned to it. "I've been in Cardiff six weeks doing a thing about a detective with a tragic past, and everyone's *lovely*, everyone's so lovely, and I haven't had a single conversation I'd remember by teatime. And you've been rude to me for four minutes and I could tell you every word of it." The shop was very quiet. The clock over the till ticked. "That's not a compliment," she said. "That's a diagnosis." "Probably." He didn't look away. "Are you going out tonight? On the river?" "It's been raining up top. She'll be coloured till Thursday." "Thursday, then." "I didn't invite you." "No. You didn't." He set the Falkus down on the counter between them, squared it with the edge like a man laying down a hand of cards. "How much?" "Forty." "For a first edition? You're robbing yourself." "I know what I'm doing." "I believe that." He put down two twenties, then a third, then a business card he'd produced from somewhere—a plain one, just a number. "For the ladder." "I don't want your money." "Then it's for the stoat's tail. Thursday. Below the bridge." He put the sunglasses back on and the bus-advert man reassembled himself, piece by piece, and she found she resented every piece. "I'll bring the bad hackles. You bring the—whatever it is that you do." "Silence, mostly." "Perfect. I'm sick of the sound of my own voice." "You aren't." "No," he admitted. "But I'd like to be." The bell went off again. Through the gap in the ladder she watched him walk straight up Rhosmaen Street toward the cameras with his collar up and his chin high, letting them have him. She stood there for a long moment. Then she took the card, looked at it, and put it in the till under the twenties, where she wouldn't have to see it until Thursday.

The Welsh setting is authentically rendered through place names (Llandeilo, Llangadog, Tywi) and local terminology ("sewin" for sea trout), creating genuine atmosphere without feeling forced or touristy. The characterization is particularly well-executed. Julian emerges as the requested "rogue with a fragile ego" - his practiced charm ("Full beam" smile) contrasts effectively with moments of genuine vulnerability (the flinch at the camera flash). The author skillfully shows his need for validation through his confusion when Nerys doesn't respond to his usual tactics. Nerys is equally well-drawn, with her dry Welsh wit and genuine expertise creating a character who feels lived-in rather than constructed for the plot. The dialogue carries the scene effectively, with distinct voices that feel natural rather than constructed. Nerys's clipped responses ("I know you're leaning on a first edition") and Julian's shifting between performative charm and genuine interest create authentic conversational rhythms. The fishing conversation serves as an excellent pivot point where both characters drop their guards. The romantic tension builds organically through shared expertise rather than forced attraction. The moment when Julian's "real" smile appears (lopsided, showing the crooked tooth) effectively contrasts with his manufactured public persona. The author shows rather than tells the growing connection through small actions - Nerys moving the ladder, Julian's genuine interest in the fishing book. The prose is clean and economical, with well-chosen details that serve multiple purposes. The "dropped coin" metaphor for Nerys's reaction to Julian's laugh is precise without being overwrought. The pacing moves naturally from the initial tension of his entrance to the quieter, more intimate fishing discussion. However, there are some minor weaknesses. The ending, while satisfying, relies somewhat on the familiar trope of the mysterious business card. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 86.8
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door gave with a sigh of old hinges, and the underhold breathed out at them: whale oil and brine, the sweetness of rendered blubber gone rancid in the lamps, and beneath it something older, mineral, like the inside of a tomb. The chamber had been built inside a ribcage. Leviathan bones arched overhead, each rib thick as a mainmast, yellowed and scrimshawed from floor to apex with the guild's history—hangings, heists, the great fire of the Ropewalk. Brass pipes threaded between them, hissing faintly. At the far end, upon a plinth of black basalt, sat the Scythan Heart in its cage of interlocking brass, dark and wet-looking as a liver. And before it, in a high-backed chair of carved bone, sat Ostrova. Aya's breath stopped in her throat. "Shut the door, dears," said the guild leader. "The draught is murder on my knees." Simeon's pocket watch ticked. Once. Twice. Ostrova had not changed her dress since the raid. There was even a smear of soot on her collar, artful as a beauty mark. She was smoking a clay pipe, and the four men ranged behind her held harpoon-guns of the naval pattern, the barbs greased and gleaming. A fifth stood in the shadow of a rib with a lantern hooded to a slit. "You were arrested," Katra said, stupidly, because someone had to. "Was I? How dreadful." Ostrova exhaled a ribbon of smoke. "Do you know, I have been running this guild for twenty-two years, and in all that time I have never once been so vulgar as to be *caught*. But I have grown old, and old women sleep poorly, and they lie awake wondering which of their children would come for the Heart if the wolf were dragged off in chains." She smiled. Her teeth were very good for a woman of the Rookery. "So I let the Watch drag a woman in my coat down Chandler's Row in the small hours, and I came down here with a bottle, and I waited. It has been a most instructive evening. You are the third party through that door." *The others,* Aya thought. *Where are the others.* She did not see bodies. She saw a dark stain near the plinth that the lamplight would not settle on. Tick. Tick. "You are the one I wanted, though," Ostrova went on, and her pale eyes found Aya's mask and stayed there. "The Nightingale. Six months in my house and none of my people can tell me the colour of your hair. The things you called up at the Custom House—Bertrand still cannot hold a spoon. I ask myself: what sort of creature learns to whistle up the dark, and then chooses to spend her evenings picking locks for *me*?" Aya felt the immateria at the edge of her, the cold seam where the world was thin. It would be nothing to reach into it. She had done it in dreams before she had ever done it awake; her mother had said the gift came like teeth, whether one wanted it or not. She let her fingers begin to curl. "Ah—no." Ostrova raised the pipe like a conductor's baton, and the man with the lantern threw back its hood. Katra jerked. There was a barb resting against the soft place beneath her jaw, held by a guard Aya had not seen at all; he had come from behind the door itself, from the dark they'd walked through. "Salt and iron," Ostrova said, almost kindly, nodding at the floor, and Aya saw it now—the pale line of it, a wide ring scuffed into the flagstones, the rusted nails hammered at intervals. "I don't pretend to understand it. Men trust what they can oil and load. But I have paid a good deal of money over the years to a great many frightened people, and they tell me it *slows* your sort. Not stops. Slows. And Tomas, there, is very quick with a spear." Tick. *I could still do it.* The thought was cold and clear. *Something would come. Something always comes.* And Katra would be dead before its first shadow touched the floor. Aya opened her hands. "Sensible girl." Ostrova gestured, and rough fingers took Aya's arms, her wrists, dragged Simeon to his knees hard enough that she heard the watch strike stone in his pocket and keep ticking regardless. "Now. Let us see what we have bought." The mask came off. The silence after was long enough for Aya to hear the whale oil guttering in the lamps. Then Ostrova stood. It cost her; the knees had not been a lie. She crossed the salt line and took Aya's chin in fingers that smelled of tobacco and ambergris, and turned her face to the light. "Oh," she said softly. "Oh, I know those eyes. I saw them at the end of a rope on Gibbet Hill, when you were what—nine? Ten? The Marchioness Halloway. They put a hood on her, and it slipped." Her thumb pressed Aya's cheekbone. "Lord Admiral Halloway's daughter. In *my* cellar. In *my* mask." Aya's heart was a fist against her stays. She saw it all, entire, in the space of a tick: the constables at her father's door. The Admiralty court. The broadsheets—*WITCH-BLOOD WILL OUT*. The particular hood they used for women of quality, and how it slipped. "You're thinking of the gallows," Ostrova said. "I'm thinking," said Aya, and was distantly proud that her voice held, "of your ledger." The pipe paused halfway to Ostrova's mouth. "You have four men, a room full of bones, and a stone you cannot sell." Aya made herself look only at the pale eyes, not the barb, not Katra's white face. "What you do not have is a friend in the Admiralty. The dockyards are tightening. The whaling fleet sails under the Lord Admiral's seal, and every cask of oil that lights your Rookery passes through his bonded warehouses. You could kill me, and tomorrow you would have three bodies and the same problems." She drew breath. "Or you could hold a witch's daughter—a *practising* witch—who would very much prefer her father never learned where she spent her evenings. And who would do a great deal to keep it so." Tick. "You're offering me your own leash," Ostrova said. "I'm telling you what I'm worth alive." *Everything I have. Everything Mother had. And I will hang for it in the end regardless, but not tonight.* "Dead, I am a scandal. Alive, I am a key." Ostrova looked at her for a long moment. Behind her, the Heart sat in its brass cage, dark and patient, as though it had heard such bargains before. "Tomas," she said at last. "Lower the spear. But keep it near." Simeon's watch ticked on in the quiet, marking out the seconds of a life that was, for now, still Aya's to lose.

The adherence to instructions is excellent - all story beats are hit naturally, the confrontation unfolds as requested without devolving into action, and the dialogue maintains period-appropriate formality. The unmasking scene and subsequent negotiation are particularly well-executed, with Aya's desperation masked by calculated reasoning. Character voices are distinct and believable. Ostrova emerges as a compelling antagonist - cunning, patient, and pragmatic rather than cartoonishly evil. Her dialogue feels authentic to someone who has survived decades leading a criminal organization. Aya's internal conflict between her aristocratic upbringing and criminal activities creates genuine tension, and her final gambit feels earned rather than convenient. The prose quality is consistently high, with evocative imagery that serves the story rather than overwhelming it. Descriptions like "The chamber had been built inside a ribcage" and the recurring motif of Simeon's pocket watch create atmosphere without becoming purple. The salt and iron circle detail shows thoughtful worldbuilding about magic's limitations. The emotional complexity is notable - Aya grapples with multiple layers of fear (discovery, death, family shame) while maintaining enough composure to negotiate. The piece successfully builds tension through pacing and reveals rather than relying on action sequences. Some minor weaknesses include occasional exposition that could be more seamlessly integrated, and Katra remains somewhat underdeveloped compared to the other characters. The ending, while appropriate to the scene, leaves several threads hanging that may feel unsatisfying as a standalone piece, though this appears intentional for a continuing narrative. The negotiation sequence particularly showcases the author's ability to convey character intelligence through speech patterns and word choice. Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Gunpowder Rendezvous** The bar has no name, only a flickering neon fish over the door and a floor that grips the soles of Spike's shoes like it wants to keep them. He slouches onto a stool, orders whatever's cheapest, and is halfway through lighting a cigarette when the woman two seats down says, "Hollowell." He pauses. The lighter in his hand—an old brass Zippo, a ring of rust around its base from more baptisms than he cares to count—keeps burning. "Sorry?" "Vince Hollowell. Eight hundred grand, dead or alive, and you've got the look." She doesn't turn her head. She's all shoulders and cutoff shorts, a dragon crawling up her right arm in green and gold ink, a cigarette parked in the corner of her mouth. "Somebody hired you to bring him in. Somebody hired me first." "First doesn't mean much." Spike finally lights up, snaps the Zippo shut. "It's a big number. Plenty of people probably got the call." "Plenty of people are dead." Now she looks at him. Her eyes are dark and flat and tired in a way he recognizes from mirrors. "Three of 'em in that alley behind the fish market. You want to make it four, be my guest." He smiles lazily and slides his glass toward the bartender for a refill. "Spike." "Revy." She lifts her rum. "Don't get attached." --- They drink because there's nothing else to do until Hollowell shows, and Hollowell always shows at the fish bar on Thursdays; it's in the file. Revy drinks like she's angry at the bottle. Spike drinks like he's already forgotten he ordered it. "So what are you," she says, "some kinda cowboy? You got that whole *nothing matters* thing going. Pisses me off." "I died once already." He shrugs, cigarette bobbing. "Everything since has been kind of a bonus round." "Bullshit." "Probably." He gestures at her holsters, twin Berettas riding low. "Two Hands, right? Heard about you. Roanapur." Something shifts in her jaw. "And I heard about you. Syndicate guy who walked out. Left a woman behind." She waits for him to flinch. He doesn't, quite, but his good eye goes somewhere far away for a second and the other one—the one that isn't real—stays exactly where it is. "Everybody leaves somebody," he says. "Yeah." She knocks back the rum. "Or somebody leaves them. Same coin." Their knees are almost touching under the bar. Neither of them moves. --- Hollowell walks in at eleven with four men and the confidence of a man who's never met either of them. Spike sees Revy's hand drift toward her hip and mutters, "Wait—" She doesn't wait. The first shot takes out the neon fish, which Spike thinks is unnecessary until he realizes she did it for the dark. Then the room comes apart. Revy's up on the bar, both pistols spitting, a shell casing hissing into somebody's drink. Spike goes low and sideways, Jericho in hand, kicks a chair into a bodyguard's knees and drops him with one round through the shoulder. Somewhere behind him Revy laughs, high and vicious, and it's the least sane sound he's heard in months and he finds himself grinning anyway. Hollowell bolts for the kitchen. Spike vaults a table to cut him off. Revy comes off the bar in a crouch and they arrive at the swinging door at exactly the same moment, shoulder to shoulder, guns raised— —at each other. Hollowell's already halfway out the back. "Move," she says. "You move." The kitchen door bangs. A car starts in the alley. They stand there, muzzles six inches apart, breathing hard, until the engine noise fades. "Well," Spike says. "That's eight hundred grand driving away." Revy shoots the wall next to his head. It's not personal. He can tell. --- They know where he's going—the file has that too, a motel on the coast road—but it's fifty miles and neither of them has a working car, so they steal one together, which is its own kind of intimacy. Revy drives. Spike smokes with his feet on the dash and watches her hands on the wheel, the way the dragon flexes when she shifts. "You're staring," she says. "Depth perception's bad. Takes me a while to figure out how far away things are." "That a line?" "Might be." She almost smiles. It's terrifying. --- The motel is a horseshoe of cinderblock around an empty pool. Hollowell's car is out front, but Hollowell isn't in room 14 where he should be; room 14 has a window open and a bathroom the size of a coffin and a bed that sags in the middle. "Son of a bitch went out the back," Revy says. "Or he's in another room." "Or he's in another room." Neither of them goes to check. The door swings shut behind them. Spike's back is to the wall and Revy's standing too close, rum and gunsmoke on her breath, and he notices with a strange detached interest that she's got one Beretta pressed lightly to his sternum and he's got the Jericho resting against the soft place under her ribs. He doesn't remember either of them drawing. "This is stupid," she says. "Yeah." "You'd shoot me for the money." "Probably not." He considers it honestly. "I'd shoot you if you shot me first." "That's the most romantic goddamn thing anyone's ever said to me." Her free hand is in his shirt, knuckles against his chest. She's shaking, very slightly, and he doesn't think it's fear. "I don't do this. Trust people. Whatever." "Me neither." "So what the hell is this?" He looks at her—the flat black eyes, the dragon, the mouth that's about to either kiss him or bite him—and thinks about a woman with yellow hair and a different kind of gun, and knows Revy's thinking about somebody too, some fool in a white shirt who followed her into the dark. "Whatever happens," Spike says, "happens." "That's not an answer." "It's the only one I've got." The guns stay where they are. The gap between them closes to nothing and stops there, an inch of hot air, neither pulling the trigger, neither closing the distance. Outside, a car door slams. Hollowell, probably, running again. Neither of them moves to catch him.
