Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Breaking Formation The speakers sit in all four corners like bouncers, and they're all playing the same track a hair too loud, so that in the exact center of the floor the bass folds over on itself and thrums in my teeth. I'm not in the center. I'm back row, far left, the spot you give the scholarship kid. Tape X under my sneakers. Mirror wall in front of me, twelve of us reflected in three neat rows of four. Instructor Yoon stands at the front, off to my right, one hand on the remote like it's a leash. "From the chorus. Five, six, seven, eight—" *One.* Right arm slices straight down, blade of the hand cutting past the hip, weight drops onto the right foot. *Two.* Left arm mirrors. Eleven bodies do it like one machine with twenty-two levers. Mine does it like a person. I can see the difference in the mirror before Yoon says anything. Jiwoo, right next to me, hits *one* dead on top of the beat—arm locks, stops, no bleed. My arm gets there on the same count but *through* something, a little ripple in the shoulder before it lands, because back home you don't stop a move, you finish it. On the Boulevard we rode the pocket. You hit a hair behind the kick so the movement had somewhere to swing. Here, behind is late. Yoon told me on day one: "Late is a choice." *Three, four.* Hip isolations, knees bent, both feet planted. Left hip snaps out, snaps back. Right hip. The room does it like a switch flipping—click, click. My hips want to roll. Ten years of muscle memory says a hip that goes out should come back around, not retract on a straight line. I fight it and the fight shows: my isolations land but my ribs keep talking, a tiny undulation that makes the reflection in the back-left corner look like it's underwater while everyone else is stone. *Five.* Pivot left on the ball of the right foot, head whips to the mirror. Now I'm facing forward again but I've turned through a full circle and I can see Yoon has moved—she's walking down the right side of the room, arms folded, watching me from the side angle. *Six.* Knee drop. Right knee to the floor, left leg bent at ninety, back straight, chin up. This is where my body betrays me every single time. A drop, where I'm from, is a *statement*. You go down heavy. Stomp, chest pop on the impact, arms flare like something exploded out of your sternum. Krump lives on that impact. And my knee hits the sprung floor and my chest pops—not big, I've been sanding it down for three weeks—but it pops, and my left arm comes up an inch higher than the choreography, a phantom of a buck that's been drilled into my spine since I was nine. "Stop." The remote clicks. The four speakers cut out mid-syllable and the silence has a shape, a pressure. Yoon crosses in front of the first row. Her shoes make no sound. She stops directly in front of my line, two rows ahead, so I'm looking at her back in the mirror and her face in reality. "You," she says. Not my name. "Count six. What happens to your chest?" "It pops." "Why?" *Because that's where the beat lives. Because a drop without impact is just kneeling.* "Habit." "Habit." She lets the word sit in the too-quiet air. Twelve trainees breathing. The girl in front of me, Minseo, hasn't moved a millimeter, still frozen on her right knee, and I'm suddenly aware of how expensive her stillness is—the years of private lessons it took to make a body that obedient. I learned on cracked asphalt with a phone speaker. My teacher was a guy named Dre who's dead now. "Habits are what people have who cannot afford training," Yoon says. "I can find your talent in any subway station in this city. I cannot use it. When the camera cuts to a wide shot, I need twelve bodies that are one body. Your chest is not one body. Your chest is a soloist." She turns to face the mirror, standing where a thirteenth dancer would be, dead center front. "Again. From five." Speakers roar back on. *Five.* Pivot. *Six.* Drop—and I lock my chest, I hold it like a breath, and the knee lands silent and my arms stay where the choreography says. In the mirror I'm identical to Jiwoo. Identical to Minseo. I feel nothing land. It's like the move never happened. *Seven.* Rise, arms crossing at the sternum, right over left. *Eight.* Hold. Then the formation shift on the *and*: back row breaks forward on diagonals. Jiwoo cuts front-right, I cut front-left, three long steps, and the rows collapse into a V with me at the front-left point, Yoon's shadow in the center. New tape X under my feet. New view: I'm now closest to the mirror, and the speaker in the front-left corner is a foot from my ear, so loud the high end is fizzing. This is the point choreography. Chorus hook. The part they'll put on the thumbnail. Eight counts of arm work so sharp it looks like animation—slice, frame, frame, punch, retract, box, box, freeze. *One.* Slice. Clean. *Two.* Frame the face, elbows squared. Clean. *Three, four.* Frame lower, punch out. My reflection is a soldier. *Five.* Retract. And I feel it coming like weather. Count six through eight is a box—arms tracing a hard square in front of the chest, then a freeze with the head tilted exactly fifteen degrees. In the eight-bar phrase this is the moment the track drops an extra kick, a syncopated ghost note buried under the synth, and every cell in my body hears it and wants to answer. A wave. Just one—fingertip to shoulder, riding that ghost kick, the thing I would have done at the Boulevard without thinking, the thing that made people circle up. I can hear Yoon in my head: *soloist*. I can hear Dre: *if you don't answer the music, why are you dancing to it?* *Six.* Box. Arms square. *Seven.* Box— The ghost kick hits. The whole room is stone. And I let my right hand go liquid for one count, the wave traveling wrist to elbow to shoulder, arriving at the freeze on *eight* in exactly the right position, head tilted exactly fifteen degrees, so that if you blinked you missed it. I didn't blink. In the mirror, over my shoulder, neither did Yoon. She lets the hold run three full seconds. Then the remote clicks and the corners go silent. "Again," she says. "And this time, decide."

+ Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 90.5
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Court of the Dreaming: The Matter of the Wildflower Field** The hourglass stood taller than the gallery, and its sand fell in a thread of pale glitter that never quite reached the bottom. Nobody could remember who had set it going. Nobody wanted to be present when it ran out. Dream sat beneath it. He had not moved for some time. "Continue," he said. First Love shuffled forward, clutching a sheaf of papers that appeared to be pressed flowers. He was pink to the ears and had been for roughly a century. "So — as I was saying, my lord — the field is *mine*. I laid the grass down blade by blade. I chose the wildflowers. Cornflowers, mostly, because Max doesn't know the names of any others and I didn't want to overwhelm him. I put a bee in it. One bee. For verisimilitude." "Noted." "The girl is Jessica Hartley from his geography class. I've been building her for eleven months. She lies beside him. There is a moment. He doesn't know what to do with his hands. She leans in, he leans in, and then —" First Love made a small gesture, like someone letting go of a balloon. "Nothing. Beautifully, perfectly nothing. He wakes up not knowing what he feels, and that's the *point*, my lord. That's the whole point. He's supposed to carry that for years." "And the defendant?" "She *sat on him*." A ripple of dry amusement went through the gallery. The gallery was made up of the usual: two Anxieties in matching suits, a Falling that kept starting from its seat, an old Recurring Staircase that had been attending hearings since before anyone had legs to climb it. Mora had not bothered to stand. She was draped over the defendant's bench like a coat someone had thrown there, all elbows and black hair and a mouth that was slightly too wide. She was, unhelpfully, beautiful. It was the sort of beauty that made you check whether you were still breathing. "Your Honour," she said. "That is not my title." "Your Dreadfulness." "Neither is that." "Your — okay. Look." She sat up, which took longer than it should have. "I'm not disputing the field. Lovely field. Nice bee. But here's the thing. I've got a route. I've had it since before the Poles were Poles. And the route's gone to hell. Nobody sleeps on their back anymore, they've all got these pillows shaped like wedges. Half my old houses are laminate flooring now — nothing to grip. So I'm out there, hungry, and I come across this kid. Fourteen. Lying in a field. On his back." She spread her hands. "A girl's gotta eat too, you know?" "That is your defence." "That's my defence." "Your entire defence." "I could dress it up, but you'd see through it, so." She shrugged. "I sit on the chest. He can't move. I take a bit of breath. He wakes up. Everybody lives." First Love was vibrating. "She *replaces Jessica*. Jessica climbs on top of him — playfully, my lord, it's a playful thing, she's tickling him — and then halfway through she becomes *that*." He pointed at Mora without looking. "The hair goes wrong. The eyes go wrong. The teeth. And she sits there, and she *inhales*, and he can't scream, and the worst part — the *worst* part —" "Go on." "He still fancies her." Silence, except for the sand. "I see," said Dream. "He does not know *what* he is supposed to feel anymore. He was meant to have a sweet, muddled confusion. Now he has a — a *different* confusion. A terrible one. He's started doing his geography homework." First Love's voice cracked. "*Voluntarily.*" Mora examined her nails, which were longer than they had been a moment ago. "Sounds like character development." "It sounds like *theft*." "You built a bed. I lay in it. Where I come from, that's not theft, that's hospitality." Dream raised one hand a fraction of an inch, and the argument stopped the way a dropped plate stops. He looked at the hourglass. He did this rarely, and everyone in the gallery noticed. The Falling fell off its seat and climbed back up. "You are both," said Dream, "wasting my time." First Love flushed a deeper shade. Mora had the decency to look slightly caught. "A dream is not owned by the one who builds it. Nor by the one who eats in it. It belongs to the sleeper, who is not here, because he is fourteen and asleep, and would in any case find these proceedings less frightening than a school assembly." He let that settle. "The field will remain. The girl will remain. The defendant may continue her visits." "My lord —" "Once a fortnight. No more. She will sit on his chest, and she will take her breath, and she will not be sloppy about it." Mora grinned. It was a good grin. It had too many corners. "However." Dream's voice did not change, but something in the room did. The old Staircase creaked, as though bracing. "The boy will remember." First Love went white, which on him was a considerable journey. "He — that's against every —" "He will remember the field. The bee. The almost. And he will remember what came after, and that he did not entirely mind. He will carry both. Into adulthood. Into every field he ever lies down in." A pause, barely there. "It will be very confusing for him. I imagine some of it will turn into poetry. Most of it will not." Mora had stopped grinning. "That's cruel." "It is *tidy*," said Dream. "You wished to feed. He wished to love. Now he will find it difficult to tell the difference. I am told that is a common condition among the waking." He rose. The hourglass sand thinned to a single glittering hair. "This court is adjourned. Do not bring me a bee again." Nobody laughed. But afterwards, in the corridor where things wait to be dreamed, First Love asked Mora whether she thought he'd been joking, and Mora said she genuinely couldn't tell, and that was rather the problem with him, wasn't it.

Lines like "She was draped over the defendant's bench like a coat someone had thrown there" and "It was the sort of beauty that made you check whether you were still breathing" are economical yet evocative. The writing maintains consistent voice throughout, with Dream's formal cadence contrasting nicely with Mora's casual irreverence. The dark comedy emerges naturally from the situation rather than forced jokes. The absurdity of bureaucratizing dream disputes, Mora's pragmatic "a girl's gotta eat" defense, and First Love's horror at voluntary geography homework all land effectively. The resolution is particularly clever, subverting expectations by giving both parties what they want while introducing a cruel twist that serves Dream's character. The ending avoids false positivity - it's neither happy nor sad but complexly unsettling, which fits the dark fantasy tone perfectly. The dialogue throughout is sharp and character-specific. Each voice is distinct, from Dream's formal pronouncements to Mora's casual deflections to First Love's passionate advocacy. The courtroom procedural elements feel authentic while maintaining the fantastical atmosphere. Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Blood Moon** A broken cart wheel lies abandoned near the village gates, its spokes splayed like the ribs of something gutted. Yennefer steps over it without slowing. Whoever fled this place did so in a hurry, and she does not blame them. The air tastes wrong. Copper and rot, layered beneath something older, something that makes the hairs along her arms lift in warning. The village is silent. No dogs. No hearth smoke. Only the moon, swollen and red, bleeding light across the thatched roofs. She has been tracking the disappearances for eleven days, following rumors of a pale stranger, a red coat, a laugh that carried across fields at midnight. The local lord paid handsomely for her to investigate. She suspects now that the coin was not worth it. "Sorceress." The voice comes from everywhere and nowhere, a purr threaded with amusement. Yennefer does not startle. She has trained herself out of startling. Instead she lifts her chin and lets Chaos gather in her fingertips, cool and coiled. "You have my attention," she says. "Try not to waste it." He steps out of the shadow of the well, and the shadow does not want to release him. It stretches, clings, drags along his boots before finally giving up. He is tall, absurdly so, draped in crimson, his hat brim low, his eyes hidden behind glass the color of dying embers. His smile is too wide. Too many teeth. "Waste it," he repeats, savoring the words. "How long has it been since anyone spoke to me that way?" "Not long enough, evidently." He laughs. The sound bounces off the empty houses and comes back wrong, doubled, as if something inside the walls is laughing with him. Yennefer studies him the way she would study an unfamiliar text. He is not human. That much is obvious. But he is not any vampire she knows either. Higher vampires are subtle, elegant, careful. This creature wears his monstrousness like a banner. "You killed them," she says. "The villagers." "Some." He tilts his head. "The ones who ran, I let run. The ones who begged, I found tedious. The ones who fought." His smile sharpens. "I enjoyed those." "How generous." "You're not afraid." "Should I be?" He moves. One moment he is beside the well, the next he is close enough that she can smell the grave on him, damp earth and old blood. She does not step back. She refuses to step back. Instead she lifts one hand and the air between them ignites, a wall of violet flame that throws his shadow twenty feet long. He walks through it. His coat smolders. His skin blackens, peels, and reknits itself before the ash can fall. He stops a breath away from her, and she sees her own reflection in his lenses, small and pale and utterly unimpressed. "Interesting," he murmurs. "I've barely started." She speaks a word that has not been spoken aloud in three centuries, and the ground beneath him opens. He drops. She seals it. For a single, satisfying heartbeat, there is quiet. Then the earth bulges, cracks, and he rises out of it in pieces, a swarm of black shapes with red eyes that reassemble into a man mid-laugh, brushing dirt from his sleeves. "Oh," he says, delighted. "Oh, *yes*." Yennefer's pulse is steady. She makes it steady. Her fingers ache from the Chaos she has already pulled through them, but she does not let them tremble. "What are you?" she asks, and hates that it comes out as a question. "A monster." He shrugs. "As are you, in your way. That perfume of yours, lilac and gooseberries. It doesn't quite cover the smell of what you did to yourself." Her jaw tightens. He sees it. Of course he sees it. "You reshaped your body," he continues, circling her now, slow and unhurried. "Carved yourself into something beautiful. Paid a price for it. I can smell the hollow where the price was taken." "Careful," she says softly. "Or what? You'll set me on fire again?" He spreads his arms. "Please." She could portal away. The thought arrives and she dismisses it in the same instant. If she flees, he wins. If she stays, she might die. Neither option is acceptable, so she chooses a third. "You could have killed me already," she says. "You haven't. Why?" He stops circling. "Because you might be worth the effort," he says, and the humor drains from his voice, leaving something raw beneath. "Do you know how long I've searched for someone who could end me? Kings. Armies. Priests with their crosses and their silver. All of them boring. All of them *weak*." "And you think I'm not." "I think you don't know what you are." He leans in. "You've been hiding from it your whole life. Tucking it behind pretty eyes and a straight spine." The slap lands before she decides to deliver it. Her palm cracks against his cheek, and the Chaos she pours through it hits like a battering ram. He goes flying. His body slams through the wall of the smithy and the roof comes down on top of him. Yennefer stands in the ruined square, breathing hard, and waits. He emerges laughing. Blood streams from his mouth, black in the red moonlight, and he licks it away with obvious relish. "There," he says. "There she is." "I'm not your entertainment." "No." He straightens his hat. "You're something rarer." For a long moment neither of them moves. The moon hangs heavy above them. Somewhere a shutter bangs in a wind that has not been blowing until now. "Leave this place," Yennefer says. "Go back to wherever you crawled from." "And if I do?" "Then I won't have to find out which of us is right about me." He considers this. She watches him consider it, and understands that she is being weighed, catalogued, remembered. "Another night, then," he says at last. "When the moon is this color again." "I'll be waiting." "I know." He folds into shadow and is gone. The village exhales. Yennefer stands alone until the trembling in her hands subsides, then turns and walks back toward the gates, past the broken wheel, and does not look back once.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and atmospheric writing. The author successfully captures the essence of both characters - Alucard's sadistic playfulness and regenerative abilities are well-portrayed, while Yennefer's pride, magical prowess, and refusal to show weakness align perfectly with her character. The medieval European setting is established efficiently through environmental details like the abandoned cart, thatched roofs, and village structure. The prose maintains a consistent dark, gothic tone throughout, with particularly effective imagery like "the moon, swollen and red, bleeding light" and "shadow does not want to release him." The power dynamic shifts are well-executed, with neither character gaining clear dominance - Yennefer's magical attacks are countered by Alucard's regeneration, while his psychological probing is met with her defiant composure. The dialogue feels authentic to both characters, capturing Yennefer's sharp wit ("Try not to waste it") and Alucard's predatory amusement. The conversation about Yennefer's transformation and the "hollow where the price was taken" demonstrates good knowledge of her backstory while serving the narrative tension. However, the piece occasionally veers toward purple prose, particularly in some of the more elaborate metaphors. The ending, while dramatically satisfying, feels somewhat predictable in its "we'll meet again" resolution. Some descriptions, while atmospheric, border on overwrought - the repeated emphasis on shadows and darkness sometimes feels heavy-handed. The pacing is generally strong, building tension through their verbal sparring and magical confrontation, though the middle section with the magical combat could have been more dynamic. The piece succeeds in showing rather than telling character traits through actions and dialogue, particularly in how both characters refuse to back down despite clear danger. + Fanfic-crossover: Prison Strings — Score: 80.9
Prompt:
Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The chain-link fences within the yard rattle whenever an inmate passes by, a nervous metallic shiver that runs the length of the enclosure like a warning nobody bothers to listen to. Jolyne Cujoh listens. She has to. Three weeks in this place has taught her that the fences here don't just rattle. Sometimes they hum. Sometimes they lean toward you. She sits on a concrete bench with her knees pulled up, picking at the butterfly on her forearm, and watches the new arrival cross the yard. The woman doesn't rattle the fence at all. That's the first thing. Everyone else, guards included, sends that shiver through the links. This one walks past a twelve-foot stretch of chain and the metal holds its breath. She wears a plain white shirt and dark slacks, not a jumpsuit, and her auburn hair swings in a low braid. She smiles at an inmate who spits near her shoes. She smiles at the tower guard. She smiles at Jolyne, and her eyes are yellow with rings inside rings, like something drawn by a hand that has never seen a real eye up close. "You're new," Jolyne says when the woman stops in front of her bench. It isn't a question and it isn't friendly. "I'm visiting," the woman says. Her voice is soft. Pleasant. The kind of voice that reads bedtime stories to children it plans to eat. "My name is Makima. I'm with Public Safety. This facility has an... arrangement with my department." "Arrangement." Jolyne rolls the word around. "Yeah. Lotta arrangements in here. My *arrangement* is fifteen years for a thing I didn't do." "I know," Makima says. "I read your file on the plane." Jolyne's fingers stop moving on her arm. "Did you." "Stone Free." Makima sits down on the far end of the bench uninvited, folding her hands in her lap like a schoolteacher. "You unravel. Into string. You can extend it, thread it through locks, listen through it, reassemble anywhere the strands reach." She tilts her head. "That's very beautiful. I'd like to see it." "Yeah, well." Jolyne unhooks a thread of herself from the inside of her wrist, just a single blue-green filament, and lets it drift in the air between them like a question mark. "I'd like to see you take a long walk off the north wall. We don't always get what we want." Makima doesn't flinch from the thread. She watches it the way a person watches a fish in a tank. "You don't like me." "I don't like people who smile with their mouths and nothing else." "That's perceptive." Makima says it as a compliment, and it lands like a compliment, and that's what makes Jolyne's skin crawl. "Most humans respond to warmth without checking where it comes from. They want to be liked so badly that they don't ask who's doing the liking." *Most humans.* Jolyne files it away. Across the yard, a big inmate named Dorsey is kicking a smaller one in the ribs. This is normal. What isn't normal is when Makima glances over, not even a full turn of the head, and Dorsey stops. Stands up straight. Walks to the fence. The fence rattles as he approaches. It rattles harder when he presses his face into it. It does not stop rattling when he starts pushing, the links biting into his cheeks, the wire beginning to open his skin, and he doesn't make a sound. "Hey!" Jolyne is on her feet. "*Hey!* Knock it off, you dumb—" "He can't hear you," Makima says mildly. "He's not in charge of himself right now." Jolyne's string is already out, ten meters of it unspooling from her palm across the dirt, whipping around Dorsey's ankle and yanking. He goes down hard, face bleeding, and lies there blinking up at the sky like a man waking from anesthesia. Jolyne reels herself back in slowly. She turns. "That was you." "That was a demonstration." Makima hasn't moved. "You wanted to know what my department does. We control things that would otherwise be uncontrollable. I'm very good at it." She smiles again. "You reacted quickly. Most people would have watched. Some part of them wants to see what happens when a face meets a fence." "You think I'm impressed?" "I think you're *interesting*." Makima stands, smoothing her slacks. She's not tall, but she stands like the yard belongs to her, like the guards in the tower are furniture she placed there. "Your string. It responds to your will completely. There's no gap between what you want and what your body does. Do you know how rare that is? Most humans spend their entire lives arguing with their own hands." Jolyne feels it then. Not a push exactly. More like a pressure at the base of her skull, gentle, patient, a hand on a dog's collar that hasn't tightened yet. *Sit,* it suggests. *Good girl. Sit.* Her legs want to. Stone Free doesn't. The string unravels from her shoulder without her deciding to, a hundred threads fanning out like a defensive net, and the pressure slides off her like rain off wire. Jolyne's teeth are bared. She didn't feel herself bare them. "Oh," Makima says quietly. Jolyne takes one step forward. Then another. The threads trail behind her in the dirt, and every strand is a nerve, and every nerve is screaming that she is standing three feet from something that is not a person, that has never been a person, that is wearing a person the way Jolyne wears her jumpsuit. "Let me tell you how this goes," Jolyne says, and her voice comes out low and steady, her father's voice climbing up out of her chest. "You don't touch my head again. You don't touch anybody in this yard again. And if you think you're gonna put a leash on me because I'm locked in a box and can't stop you—" She holds up her hand, and the thread between her fingers is taut enough to cut. "I've unraveled through worse cages than this. I'll unravel through you." Makima studies her for a long moment. Her expression doesn't change. It doesn't need to. "You aren't beneath me," she says finally. It sounds like genuine surprise. "I couldn't find where to hold you." Then, with a small, delighted breath: "How wonderful. I'll have to come back." She walks away toward the gate. The fence beside her stays perfectly silent. Behind her, Jolyne's hands are shaking, and she lets them, because the alternative is pretending they aren't. Dorsey sits up in the dirt and asks what happened. Jolyne doesn't answer. She's already threading a single strand through the chain-link, feeling for the vibration of footsteps, memorizing the shape of the one that leaves no trace.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and character understanding. The author successfully captures both Jolyne's hot-headed, suspicious nature and Makima's manipulative, inhuman demeanor. The supernatural prison setting is well-established through atmospheric details like the fence that "rattles" for normal people but stays silent around Makima. The characterization is particularly strong. Jolyne's voice feels authentic - her wariness, her protective instincts toward other inmates, and her defiant stance against authority all ring true. The author effectively shows her Stand ability through action rather than exposition. Makima is portrayed with appropriate menace, her false pleasantness masking genuine threat. The line "Most humans respond to warmth without checking where it comes from" perfectly captures her predatory nature. The prose quality is high, with evocative imagery like "her eyes are yellow with rings inside rings, like something drawn by a hand that has never seen a real eye up close." The pacing builds tension effectively, from initial suspicion to the demonstration of power to the final confrontation. The dialogue feels natural and character-appropriate. Jolyne's crude directness contrasts well with Makima's soft-spoken manipulation. The escalation feels earned - Jolyne's resistance to Makima's control ability creates genuine stakes and conflict. However, the piece occasionally veers toward overwrought description, particularly in the final confrontation where phrases like "something that is not a person, that has never been a person, that is wearing a person the way Jolyne wears her jumpsuit" feel slightly excessive. The ending, while dramatically satisfying, resolves perhaps too neatly with Jolyne's complete resistance to Makima's power. The story adheres well to the prompt requirements, maintaining third person present tense throughout and hitting the requested word count. The supernatural prison setting is utilized effectively, and both characters remain true to their source material while engaging in a compelling battle of wills. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 81.8
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-7449 **Object Class:** Euclid (provisional) **Special Containment Procedures:** All handwritten material recovered from the workspace, residence, or person of Researcher Idris Vane is to be sealed in Faraday-lined document sleeves and catalogued by Site-41 Archives. Researcher Vane has been removed from active duty and assigned to observed quarters. Any contained entity at Site-41 with documented cognitive-influence capability is subject to weekly Hume-baseline review until the origin of SCP-7449 is determined. **Description:** SCP-7449 designates a series of twenty-three handwritten notes, purportedly authored by Researcher Vane at an unspecified future date, warning of a containment breach in Wing C that has not occurred. The following account was compiled from Researcher Vane's incident statement and personal log, submitted at their own request. --- **Statement of Researcher I. Vane:** The first one was folded inside my badge holder. I found it on a Tuesday, between the plastic and the photo, and I remember laughing because the handwriting was mine. Not close to mine. Mine—the way I dropped the crossbar on the *t*, the way I never closed my *a*. > *Idris. Check the pressure seals on C-9 before the 14th. Don't let Marcus run the diagnostic alone. You'll understand later. —I.V.* I assumed a prank. Someone in Records had access to my signature. I reported it anyway, because that is what we are trained to do, and Security spent forty minutes reviewing badge-station footage. Nobody had touched my lanyard. I had put it on that morning myself. The second appeared four days later, under my keyboard. > *Marcus is already compromised. Do NOT tell him about these. The seals fail on the 14th at 03:12. Twelve dead in the first hour. I'm sorry I didn't listen either.* The 14th came. I ran the diagnostic myself, with two guards present and Marcus watching from behind glass. The seals held. Nothing happened at 03:12. I went home and slept nine hours and woke feeling foolish and relieved. Then I found the third note inside a sealed evidence bag in my desk drawer. The bag had been catalogued and heat-sealed by Archives eleven days earlier. Its chain-of-custody tape was intact. > *It didn't happen because you changed it. Good. But it moves. It always moves. Now it's the 22nd and it's C-4 not C-9 and Marcus isn't the problem anymore, the problem is the thing under the floor. Look at the sixth tile from the door. Don't let them tell you what you're seeing.* That was when Dr. Okonkwo took over. She was fair about it. She said the same thing I would have said: there were two hypotheses, and both had to be pursued with equal seriousness. Either I was receiving genuine retrocausal communication—rare, but not without precedent in Foundation records—or something at Site-41 had reached into my head and was making me write these notes myself, or making me *find* them, or making me believe I found them. They put me under observation. Cameras on my desk, my quarters, my locker. Motion-sensitive, timestamped, redundant. They sampled my handwriting under supervision and had graphologists compare it. Ninety-four percent concordance—high, but the six percent troubled them. The strokes in the later notes were pressed harder, and the letterforms drifted in ways consistent with either fatigue or, as one analyst wrote, "a hand that has forgotten some of what it knows." Then they analyzed the ink. I remember Okonkwo reading the report aloud. Site-41 stocks four pen models, all catalogued. The ink in the notes matched none of them. It contained iron gall—an archaic formulation no longer manufactured for commercial pens—and trace concentrations of strontium-90 and a cesium isotope ratio that, according to the physics annex, "does not correspond to any terrestrial source sampled since 1963." Someone had written those notes with a pen that shouldn't exist, dipped in ink from a place that shouldn't either. That was not something I could have done to myself. That was the argument I made. I made it loudly. Okonkwo pointed out that if a Site-41 entity could alter my perception, it could alter a mass spectrometer's, or the technician reading it, or her reading it to me. I asked her how anyone was supposed to function under that reasoning. She said: *carefully*. The notes kept coming. The cameras never caught them appearing. They were simply *there* when the footage was reviewed, present in one frame and absent in the frame before, with no intervening motion. Technical filed it as a recording artifact. I do not believe it was. > *the 22nd was wrong too. i'm sorry. there's no calendar where i am now. the walls are C wing but the numbers on the doors are in a script i don't know and marcus is here but he says he never worked with you and he has your face. check under the tile. CHECK UNDER THE TILE.* They checked under the tile. Sixth from the door, C-4. Concrete. They cored it two meters down to be sure. Concrete, then bedrock, then nothing. > *there is no site 41. there was never a wing c. you are in a room and the room is very small and someone is reading this to you and you should not* That note was found in my jacket pocket. I had been wearing the jacket for six hours, in full view of two guards. I want to be clear about something for the record. I know the shape of what Okonkwo suspects. She has not said the words, but I have read the same files she has—the memetic hazards, the entities that write in your hand and speak in your voice and want, more than anything, for you to trust the letter over the room. I know that the most persuasive thing a warning can do is fail to come true, because then you believe it was heeded. I also know that the ink is wrong. I have held the report. The strontium is real, or it is not, and I cannot tell which, and neither can anyone I can ask. The last note came this morning. It was under my pillow. It was very short. > *idris. stop reading these.* I have not found another since. I do not know whether that means I listened, or whether something is waiting for me to stop looking. I am submitting this so that someone other than me is holding it. *—I.V.* --- **Addendum 7449-1:** Following submission of this statement, Researcher Vane requested and was granted amnestic evaluation. Evaluation was deferred by Dr. Okonkwo pending resolution of a single unanswered question: the sample of Vane's supervised handwriting, sealed and catalogued on the day of intake, was re-examined during ink analysis. It contained iron gall and strontium-90. Site-41 stocks no such pen.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP report demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of the Foundation universe while delivering a compelling psychological horror narrative. The author successfully captures the clinical, bureaucratic tone characteristic of SCP documentation while weaving in deeply personal elements through the researcher's first-person account. The structure is expertly crafted, beginning with standard containment procedures before transitioning into the researcher's statement, creating an effective contrast between institutional objectivity and personal terror. The progression of notes shows genuine escalation - from practical warnings to increasingly fragmented and reality-questioning messages that effectively blur the line between temporal anomaly and psychological manipulation. The writing demonstrates strong technical competence in maintaining the SCP format while building genuine tension. The ink analysis detail (iron gall, strontium-90, cesium isotopes) adds scientific credibility that grounds the supernatural elements. The final revelation that the researcher's own supervised handwriting sample contains the same impossible ink creates a perfect circular trap that exemplifies good horror writing. Character development is subtle but effective within the constraints of the clinical format. Vane's voice comes through clearly - methodical, self-aware, increasingly desperate but maintaining professional composure. Dr. Okonkwo serves her role well as the rational investigator, and her reasoning about perception manipulation is logically sound within the universe. The prose is clean and purposeful, avoiding purple language while maintaining atmospheric tension. The dialogue, though limited, feels natural and serves the narrative efficiently. The piece shows rather than tells its horror through the progression of evidence and the researcher's growing uncertainty. However, the piece has some limitations. The concept, while well-executed, follows familiar SCP and time-loop horror tropes without significant innovation. The ending, though effective, doesn't quite achieve the devastating impact it reaches for. Some middle sections could be tighter, and the emotional complexity, while present, remains somewhat surface-level due to the clinical format constraints. + Scp: Unmarked Doors Archive — Score: 83.7
Prompt:
Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization. Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-7411 **Object Class:** Keter **Special Containment Procedures:** All confirmed SCP-7411 instances are to be welded shut and the surrounding structure acquired or demolished under municipal cover. Satellite and drone sweeps of abandoned structures in affected regions are to be conducted quarterly. Exploration of SCP-7411-A is suspended pending review by the Ethics Committee. All recovered documents are classified Level 5 and held at Site-01. **Description:** SCP-7411 refers to a series of identical, unmarked steel doors that manifest in derelict buildings worldwide. Instances have appeared in a shuttered textile mill in Łódź, a flooded metro station beneath Buenos Aires, a collapsed grain elevator in Saskatchewan, and forty-one other locations. Doors are consistently 2.1 meters tall, painted a flaking institutional green, and fitted with a brass handle worn smooth at the grip. In every case, the door exhibits weathering inconsistent with its surroundings. A door discovered in a Detroit factory built in 1961 shows oxidation patterns consistent with several centuries of exposure. Metallurgical analysis suggests the steel predates modern smelting techniques while conforming to no known historical alloy. Each door opens onto SCP-7411-A: a single contiguous archive of indeterminate size. Interior geometry is non-Euclidean; corridors intersect at angles exceeding 360 degrees, and stairwells have been observed to descend into rooms located above their point of origin. Shelving extends beyond the range of thermal and radar imaging. Documents are stored in cardstock folders, boxed and labeled in a script that Foundation linguists have determined to be a direct ancestor of every extant writing system. --- **Addendum 7411-1: Exploration Log 7411-A-3** *Team: Mobile Task Force Rho-9 ("Bookbinders"). Entry via Łódź instance. Three personnel: Cmdr. Adair, Agent Vukov, Dr. Halloran.* The team proceeded 400 meters along Corridor Alpha before reaching the first intersection. Adair noted that the ceiling lights, though functional, were connected to no visible wiring. Dr. Halloran began sampling documents. The first legible folder contained a bound report, approximately 200 pages, describing a "Global Cascading Breach Event." Excerpt follows: > *...containment of Designation 001 was compromised at 0417 local. Secondary sites reported concurrent failures within eleven minutes. The Directorate has authorized the Archival Protocol. All records of the current epoch are to be transferred to the Repository before the Threshold is reached. We will not survive this. The next ones must know what we knew.* Halloran observed that the document used the term "Directorate" throughout and referenced an organizational structure of Sites, Task Forces, and a thirteen-member governing body. Vukov reported that his radio was picking up faint transmissions in a language he described as "almost Russian." At 900 meters, the team entered a chamber Adair estimated at several hectares. Shelving rose beyond visible range. Halloran located a section labeled with a symbol resembling the Foundation insignia with the arrows reversed. Contents were personnel files. The first file retrieved bore a photograph of Dr. Halloran. The document was dated, per Halloran's translation, roughly 1,400 years prior to present. Excerpt: > *HALLORAN, M. — Senior Researcher, Anomalous Textiles Division. Clearance 3. Note: Subject has requested reassignment following the loss of her sister in the Site-19 incident. Request denied. Subject remains essential.* Halloran confirmed that her sister is alive and that she has never been assigned to a textiles division. She then confirmed that she has considered requesting reassignment, and that the handwriting in the marginalia was her own. Additional files were recovered for Cmdr. Adair, Agent Vukov, Site Director Okonkwo, and 211 other current Foundation personnel. All were dated to the same approximate period. Several bore a red stamp translated as "Recovered — Cycle Prior." At 1,400 meters, Vukov reported movement. The team observed six humanoid figures approximately 60 meters ahead, dressed in sealed suits of an unfamiliar white material, faces obscured by reflective visors. The figures were loading boxes onto a wheeled platform. An entire section of shelving behind them had been stripped bare. Adair ordered the team forward and identified themselves. The figures stopped, turned in unison, and ran. They abandoned the platform. Vukov pursued for 200 meters before the figures passed through a doorway that, upon Vukov's arrival, opened onto solid masonry. The abandoned platform contained fourteen boxes. All were labeled with the reversed insignia. Halloran opened one. Excerpt from top document: > *Minutes of the Thirteen, emergency session. Motion to withhold Cycle records from lower clearance passed 9–4. Rationale: knowledge of the recurrence will compromise operational will. Dissent recorded by Seats Four, Six, Eleven, Twelve. Seat Four has requested this dissent be preserved in the Repository. Motion to strike the request passed 9–4.* Adair terminated the exploration and returned to the entry point with all fourteen boxes. --- **Addendum 7411-2: Exploration Log 7411-A-6** *Team: MTF Rho-9. Entry via Buenos Aires instance. Four personnel.* At 300 meters, the team encountered a fresh boot print in dust that Halloran estimated had not been disturbed in centuries. Tread pattern matched Foundation-issue footwear. A second print, and then a third, formed a trail leading to a reading table. On the table: a ceramic mug, half full of coffee still warm, and an open folder. Adjacent to the folder, a Foundation access badge. Level 5. The name field had been scraped off with a blade, but the embedded chip read as active. Site-01 issue. The open folder contained a single page: > *To whoever finds this and is not us:* > > *We have read the Cycle records. We have read them four times now, once each time the doors return. Each time we decide the same thing. Each time we send the teams to remove what the next Directorate does not need to know. Each time we tell ourselves it is mercy.* > > *You will find your own file here. Do not read it. It does not end differently.* Vukov reported that the hazmat entities were visible at the end of the corridor, motionless, watching. When Adair took a step toward them, they turned away and resumed loading boxes. They did not run. Halloran collected the badge and the mug. Adair ordered withdrawal. --- **Addendum 7411-3:** Chip analysis of the recovered badge identifies it as belonging to O5-█. No authorization for SCP-7411-A access exists on record. When queried, O5-█ declined to respond. A subsequent Council vote to reclassify SCP-7411 as Thaumiel and cease all exploration passed 9–4. Dr. Halloran has requested reassignment. Request denied.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP entry demonstrates strong adherence to the Foundation's clinical documentation style while weaving a compelling narrative of cyclical apocalypse and institutional memory. The author successfully captures the bureaucratic tone characteristic of SCP entries, maintaining consistency throughout the technical descriptions and exploration logs. The piece excels in its structural execution, following SCP format conventions precisely while incorporating all requested elements: the mysterious doors, the impossible archive, references to a previous civilization, personnel files for current staff, and unauthorized O5 Council access. The exploration logs effectively build tension and reveal information organically through the team's discoveries. The writing demonstrates sophisticated world-building through subtle details like the reversed Foundation insignia, the "Directorate" terminology, and the implication of cyclical civilizations. The concept of the Foundation unknowingly repeating the same patterns as their predecessors creates genuine existential dread. The hazmat entities' behavior evolution from fleeing to watching adds an unsettling progression. Character actions remain believable within the SCP universe's parameters. Dr. Halloran's academic curiosity, Commander Adair's tactical decisions, and the O5 Council's secretive behavior all align with established Foundation characterization. The detail of Halloran recognizing her own handwriting in marginalia is particularly effective. The prose maintains clinical precision without becoming dry, using technical language to enhance rather than obscure the horror elements. Descriptions like "corridors intersect at angles exceeding 360 degrees" effectively convey the impossible geometry without overwrought explanation. The ending achieves genuine darkness through the implication that the Foundation is trapped in an endless cycle of making the same catastrophic decisions. The final line "Dr. Halloran has requested reassignment. Request denied" creates a chilling echo of the ancient personnel file, suggesting the cycle continues. However, the piece occasionally relies on telling rather than showing, particularly in exposition about the doors' properties. Some character development remains surface-level due to the clinical format constraints, though this is somewhat inherent to the SCP genre. + Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 86.3
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Offworlder** *From the report of Envoy Tesse Harun to the Council of the Ekumen, Cycle 93, Ansible relay from Oreth* They had told me the colony's Long People did not mix with the Short. This was in the briefing, in the second folio, under *Social Organization*, and I had read it three times on the ship and believed it, because I was twenty-six and had never yet learned that a folio is only a kind of hope arranged in columns. I left the Residency by the kitchen stair at the hour they call *thinwater*, when the reflected light off the salt flats goes grey and the delegations were still asleep after the night's speeches. Protocol forbade it. I knew that. I told myself I was going to look at the drainage, which was a lie of the sort one tells to keep one's own respect. Oreth is a heavy world, and its people have been bred by it. Twelve hundred years of gravity a fifth again greater than the human norm made the Short People: broad, deep-chested, with wrists like the roots of trees. The Long People came later, from a different ship, or so their histories say, and kept to the upland terraces where the air was poor, and they grew tall and spare and pale-eyed, with lungs that take in twice what mine can. Whether they are truly separate stocks or only two ends of one long argument with the planet, our geneticists could not agree. The Orethi themselves have no such difficulty. They know exactly who is who. I wore my cloak. It was foolish. The Orethi go bare-armed in that climate, the Short in a kind of harness of woven cord and little else, the Long in loose sleeveless tunics to the knee, and here came an offworlder in a dark wool cloak that fell to the ankles, sweating, holding it closed at the throat as though it were the last of my dignity. Children looked. A woman selling salt-fish looked, and then looked at her neighbor, and they both laughed, not unkindly, the way one laughs at a bird that has flown into a house. I bought bread from a Short woman at a stall. Her daughter handed me the change, and her daughter was Long — a head and a half taller than her mother, narrow, with the pale flat eyes of the terraces. I must have stared. The mother said, "She takes after her father," in the plain tone in which one says the weather is dry. I walked for two hours. I counted, because I am trained to count. In the market of the lower quarter I saw eleven households where both stocks lived under one roof, three where the Long served the Short, none where the reverse was true, and one where an old Long man sat in a doorway mending a Short child's harness with hands that shook. The briefing said the Long People were the ruling caste. In the lower quarter they were carrying water. When I came back the message light was already burning. Command did not shout. Command on an ansible never shouts; there is a lag of a fraction of a second that drains the heat from everything, so that you are always being scolded by someone slightly in your past. Mobile Ogura told me I had endangered the mission, the Residency, and my own person, and that it was not for the Envoy to gather data, the Envoy being a symbol and not an instrument. Then she said: "The Minister of Science has asked for you. This afternoon. You will go. You will not wear the cloak." "Minister of Science," I said. "The briefing says he was a grain factor." "The briefing," said Ogura, "is a document. He is a man. Find out which one is lying." His name was Aldo Vennerith, and he was Long, and he received me in a room with no chairs, which I later learned is an Orethi courtesy: one does not make the guest look up. We stood. He had the pale eyes and the long bones, and he wore the sleeveless tunic, and he looked at my bare arms with an expression of mild approval, as though I were a student who had finally read the assignment. "You went into the lower quarter," he said. "I did." "In a cloak." He let that sit. "Tell me, Envoy, what did you see?" I understood that this was the examination, and that everything I said would be weighed and stored and used. I thought of Ogura. I thought of the folio. I said: "I saw that your census is wrong." He did not smile. "Our census is a political document. All censuses are. Yours told you we were two peoples." "Aren't you?" "We are two peoples when it is useful to be two, and one when it is useful to be one. Is that so different from the Ekumen? Eighty worlds, and you call it a household." He moved a step, unhurried. "You are very young. They sent us someone young. I have been trying to decide whether that is an insult or a compliment." "Perhaps it is neither. Perhaps they sent what they had." "No one sends what they have. They send what they mean." He looked at me. "So. What do you mean, Envoy Harun?" I have thought since about what I might have said. Something about union, about the ansible, about the long slow patience of the Ekumen, which asks nothing and waits a thousand years. What I said was: "I mean that I bought bread this morning from a woman whose daughter does not look like her, and neither of them thought it worth remarking. I mean that I would like to know why your government thinks it worth remarking." The silence went on a while. Then Vennerith did smile, but only with the eyes. "You were told I was a grain factor," he said. "Yes." "I was. A good one. One learns, moving grain, that what you call a thing on the manifest and what arrives in the hold are seldom the same. Come back in three days. Wear whatever you like." I went back to my rooms and did not send the report for a long time. I sat with the cloak across my knees like something I had outgrown, and looked out at the salt flats going gold, and tried to decide which of us had passed.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of Ursula K. Le Guin's distinctive style and thematic preoccupations. The author successfully captures Le Guin's anthropological approach to science fiction, her measured prose rhythm, and her interest in cultural complexity and political nuance. The narrative structure follows the prompt faithfully, moving from the unauthorized exploration through the reprimand to the challenging conversation with the Minister. The framing device of a report to the Ekumen immediately establishes the Le Guin universe and provides authentic context. The world-building is economical yet rich, establishing the physical and social dynamics of Oreth through concrete details rather than exposition. The distinction between Long and Short peoples, their supposed separation, and the reality the envoy discovers creates meaningful tension that drives both plot and theme. The characterization of Tesse Harun is particularly strong - a young diplomat whose inexperience shows in small details (the inappropriate cloak, the naive belief in briefings) while demonstrating growing wisdom. The voice feels authentic to Le Guin's protagonists: observant, self-aware, and capable of growth. Minister Vennerith emerges as a compelling figure in limited space. His dialogue feels natural and carries weight, revealing character through indirection. The grain factor background provides concrete grounding for his political philosophy about the gap between official categories and reality. The prose style successfully emulates Le Guin's measured cadence and philosophical undertones. Phrases like "a folio is only a kind of hope arranged in columns" and "what you call a thing on the manifest and what arrives in the hold are seldom the same" capture her aphoristic quality without feeling forced. The thematic content engages with classic Le Guin concerns: the complexity of cultural identity, the inadequacy of official narratives, and the education of a young protagonist through direct experience. The piece avoids simple resolutions while suggesting meaningful development. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the Le Guin pastiche becomes slightly self-conscious, and the ending, while appropriate, could have pushed the emotional complexity slightly further. The pacing is generally strong though some transitions feel slightly abrupt. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 79.5
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Polymerase Chain Reaction The thermocycler was a car heater core, a peltier plate off a dead mini-fridge, and an Arduino that Vesh had soldered back to life four times. It ticked through its cycles like something with a heart condition. Ninety-four degrees. Fifty-five. Seventy-two. Denature, anneal, extend. Thirty times, and if the reagents held and the power didn't brown out, she'd have a billion copies of a gene that would otherwise be dust by Thursday. That was the whole trade now: copying things before they forgot themselves. She racked the tubes—cut-down syringe barrels, heat-sealed at the tip—and reached for the master mix. It lived in a canister the size of a coffee tin, the blue Halcyon Agrigenics helix still legible under the scratches. *GROWING TOMORROW, TODAY.* Halcyon had grown tomorrow, all right. Grown it, patented it, and set it to expire. Every seed they sold carried a sunset sequence: methylation cascades that triggered in the second generation, chopping the genome into confetti so you'd have to buy again. Corn, wheat, soy, rice. The whole planet's dinner on a subscription plan. Then the subscription ended, and so did the corporation, and so, more or less, did everything else. Vesh had eleven Halcyon canisters. Buffer in one. Primers in another. Dried DNA ladder in the smallest, which had once held a growth hormone for salmon. Salvage etiquette said you didn't ask what a container used to be. You just cleaned it with bleach and prayed. The knock on the greenhouse door came at the fourth cycle. "It's open," she said. It was always open. The lock had gone into the centrifuge—a salad spinner with a drill motor, balanced by whatever was heaviest in the room. The courier who came in was thin the way everyone was thin, but he wore it better. Clean coat. Boots that matched. He looked at the gel box—an old lunch container with copper wire electrodes—and then at her, at the scabbed patches on her scalp where the hair had given up, and said nothing about either. That told her who he worked for. Marrow's people were trained to not-notice. "You're the one who unlocked the Deng barley," he said. "I'm the one who *rebuilt* the Deng barley. Three years. Nine hundred generations of a thing that was designed to have one." She didn't look up from the tubes. "What's the contract?" He set a sample bag on her bench. Inside, a single grain of rice, mummified brown. "Halcyon Aurora Nine. The gold rice. Pre-collapse, the real line." Vesh felt her pulse do something unprofessional. Aurora Nine. Vitamin A, drought-tolerant, salt-tolerant, everything-tolerant. The seed that was supposed to save the Global South and instead put it in debt. Nobody had grown it in a decade. The stock had all sunsetted. "It's dead," she said. "It's degraded. Mr. Marrow was told there's a difference." There was. Barely. A sunset genome didn't vanish; it fragmented. If you were fast, if you had good primers and better luck, you could amplify the fragments before they slid past the point of no return and stitch them back into something a plant would recognize. The Deng barley had taken three years because she'd started with rotten seed and no polymerase worth the name. "What's the pay?" He unzipped his coat. Inside, in a rack cut from foam, sat six glass vials with intact factory seals. She read the label twice. Recombinant Taq. Not the swamp-brewed enzyme she'd been coaxing out of hot-spring bacteria in a fish tank behind the compost, half-active on a good day. The real thing, cold-chain, from before. "That's a year of work," she said. "For me. For anyone." "Mr. Marrow can wait a year. He'd like the sunset sequence left intact." And there it was. Vesh's gums had bled that morning—they did most mornings now, one of the gifts of the Chimera line she'd put into her own arm two winters ago. A Halcyon retinal therapy, never approved, meant for night-shift workers. She'd taken it because she was going blind from staring at gels under a UV lamp with no shielding. The therapy had cost her hair, her fingernails, a fever that lasted six weeks and left her joints sounding like gravel. But now, in a dark room, she could see the faint violet glow of ethidium bromide in a gel without a transilluminator. She could look at a tube of amplified DNA and *know* it had worked before she ever ran it out. Marrow's own medics had probably told him she was dying. She probably was. Everyone was. Slower than the seeds, at least. "He wants to sell rice that doesn't breed true," she said. "He wants to sell rice that people come back for." The courier said it without inflection. "It's the model that worked." "Worked." She laughed, and it hurt her mouth. "Look around." He looked. Cracked panes patched with soy-plastic. The heater-core thermocycler ticking on. Twenty flats of barley seedlings that would, this year and next and forever, make more barley. The Arduino chirped. Cycle eight. Vesh pulled on her gloves—nitrile, washed and reused until they were the texture of old skin—and lifted the rice grain out of its bag with forceps. "I'll take the contract," she said. "And the Taq." He nodded, started to zip his coat. "And I'll pull the sunset when I rebuild it," she said. "Because I don't know how to do the job otherwise. Nobody does. You want it intact, the fragments have to *be* intact, and they aren't. That's what degraded means." She met his eyes. "Tell Marrow the rice will breed true. Tell him he'll have the only Aurora Nine on the continent for exactly one season, and then every settlement he sells to will have it forever, and he should price accordingly. He can be the man who sold the last subscription or the man who sold the first free thing. Either way he's rich." The courier considered her for a long moment. Then he set the vials on the bench, one by one, each glass tap loud in the ticking room. "Ninety days," he said. "For a proof of germination." "Ninety days." When he was gone she stood in the greenhouse dark and looked at the dead grain in her forceps. She could almost see it: the faint violet ghost of everything Halcyon had meant to let rot. She dropped it into the extraction buffer, in a canister that had once held their trademark, and began, again, to copy what was left before it was gone.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This biopunk story demonstrates strong technical writing and worldbuilding within the specified parameters. The author successfully creates a post-apocalyptic setting where corporate genetic engineering with built-in obsolescence has led to societal collapse, centering the narrative around biohacker Vesh and her salvaged laboratory equipment. The worldbuilding is particularly effective, with convincing details about jury-rigged scientific equipment (the thermocycler made from car parts, the salad spinner centrifuge) and the corporate backstory of Halcyon Agrigenics. The technical aspects of PCR and genetic degradation are handled with apparent expertise, lending authenticity to the scientific elements. Vesh emerges as a compelling protagonist with clear motivations and a distinct voice. Her physical deterioration from untested genetic modifications (bleeding gums, hair loss, joint problems) contrasted with unexpected benefits (enhanced night vision) effectively illustrates the story's themes about desperate adaptation. Her moral stance against perpetuating exploitative genetic locks provides character depth. The prose maintains a consistent, gritty tone throughout, with economical yet evocative descriptions. Phrases like "copying things before they forgot themselves" and "methylation cascades that triggered in the second generation, chopping the genome into confetti" demonstrate both poetic sensibility and scientific understanding. The black market contract plot unfolds naturally, with appropriate tension and stakes. The courier's interaction with Vesh reveals character through dialogue and subtext rather than exposition. Vesh's final decision to remove the sunset sequence despite the contract terms provides a satisfying moral resolution that feels earned rather than forced. However, the story occasionally relies on technical exposition that, while accurate, can feel dense for general readers. Some descriptions border on overly technical without sufficient emotional grounding. The ending, while thematically appropriate, arrives somewhat abruptly and could benefit from more emotional resonance. The dialogue serves its purpose but lacks distinctive character voices - both Vesh and the courier speak in similar, somewhat formal registers. The story also follows a fairly predictable arc of moral choice, though it executes this familiar structure competently.
